chapters.title: Dedication
paragraphs: You've come again, you hovering shapes—I see you now, just as you first appeared to my clouded eyes back then. Should I try, this time, to catch and hold you fast? Does that old illusion still have such a grip on my heart? You're crowding closer now. Then let your reign be granted—sway me out of your misty, shadowy realm! My chest is trembling with a youthful passion, stirred by the magic breezes that rise around your approach.

You bring with you the blissful vision of joyful days gone by; the dear, familiar ghosts rise again, and, like an old, half-forgotten story, first love returns, with friendship following behind. Pain too returns renewed: with mournful repetition life traces its winding, labyrinthine path, and names the good people whose treacherous fortune tore them from happy hours and left me to grieve for them.

They no longer hear these later verses, the souls to whom I sang my earliest songs: that friendly circle is scattered, its pleasures gone, and alas, only the first echoes still ring! I offer my treasures to an unknown crowd; even their applause gives my heart a pang, and those others whose delight once flattered my song, if they're still alive, are scattered wide across the world.

And now a long-unaccustomed yearning grips me for that serene and solemn spirit-realm; my song, turning to faint wind-harp murmurs, sways like a harp-string stirred by the breeze. I shiver and tremble; tear after tear burns down; and my stern heart softens, unmanned with tenderness. What I possess I see lying far in the distance, and what I've lost becomes real and everlasting.

chapters.title: Prelude on the Stage
paragraphs: [The Theater Manager, the Poet, and the Clown.]

MANAGER. You two have often lent me a hand in hard times and trouble. Tell me now—what do you expect from this venture of ours here on German soil? I want the audience to feel well treated, especially since they keep me alive by coming. The posts are up, the wooden stage is built, and everyone's waiting for the feast I'm about to serve them. They're already sitting there, eyebrows raised with curiosity, hoping to be amazed. I know how to flatter the crowd's taste well enough, but here's my real problem: it's not that what they're used to is so demanding—it's that they've read an enormous amount already. How do we make sure everything feels fresh and new, weighty yet still entertaining? Because nothing pleases me more than watching them surge forward when the crowd starts pouring toward our theater, pushing and shoving again and again through the narrow gate of admission. Even in broad daylight they cram and jostle to reach the ticket booth, fighting like a mob, the way starving people mob a baker's door for bread, nearly breaking their necks to get a ticket. Only the poet can work that kind of miracle on such a mixed crowd—so now, my friend, show me you can do it.

POET. Don't talk to me about that motley mob out there—just the sight of them snuffs out the fire of poetry in me! Keep that surging crowd out of my sight, the one that drags us along in its whirlpool! No—lead me instead to some place of heavenly quiet, where the purer joys that belong to the poet still gather, where love and friendship still shape, in a divine way, the bonds that bless us and the wreaths that crown our passion! Ah, everything that timid lips have ever haltingly managed to say from the depths of feeling—sometimes failing, sometimes perhaps succeeding—gets swallowed by the greedy jaws of the passing moment. Or, more often, only after years of reluctant testing does its full and perfect stature finally stand revealed. What merely dazzles spends itself in the moment; what is genuine will be inherited by posterity.

MERRY-ANDREW. Posterity! Don't even mention the word to me! If I started preaching about posterity, who'd be left to provide the fun for people alive right now? Like it or not, people want that fun, and there's no getting around it. A lively, engaging young fellow, to my mind, is worth something to everybody. Someone who can pour out his nature freely takes no offense at the moods of the crowd—the wider the circle he wins over, the more solidly his inspiration works. So buck up, and give us something worth real coin! Let imagination come dressed with all her attendants—sense, reason, feeling, and passion joining in—but take care not to leave out Folly!

MANAGER. Above all, give us plenty of incident! People come to look, and what they like best is to gawk. Spin out a whole tangle of threads before their eyes, so they stare in dumb wonder—then, simply by sheer abundance, you'll have won them over, and you'll be the most popular man alive at once. Only by giving them quantity do you reach the whole crowd, because in the end everyone picks out his own favorite bit. Offer plenty, and you offer something to everyone, and each person goes home satisfied with what he found. If you've got a full piece, just serve it up in pieces—a hash, a stew—believe me, that's what succeeds! It's easy to put together and easy to invent. What's the use of presenting a tidy, unified whole? Your audience will pick it apart the moment they get their hands on it anyway!

POET. You don't feel how such a trade cheapens a person—how badly it suits a true and proud artist! I see now that this botched, patchwork approach that every second-rate hack goes in for is practically your creed.

MANAGER. That reproach doesn't bother me in the least. A man who wants to get something done has to use whatever tool actually fits the job. Remember—you've been handed soft wood to split, so think about who you're writing for! One man comes in bored, worn out completely; another leaves the table stuffed and satiated; and worst of all, plenty of them come straight from reading the day's newspapers. They drift in to us idly, the way they'd drift to a masquerade, driven by nothing but curiosity. The ladies come to show off themselves and their finery, performing their part for free. What are you dreaming of, up there in your lofty poetic perch? Does it please you to see a full house? Come closer, take a good look at your patrons' faces! Half of them are coarse, the other half are cold. One goes home to play cards once the show's over; another spends a wild night on some girl's chest. Why, you foolish poets, would you wear yourselves out chasing the gracious Muses for the sake of people like that? I tell you—give them more, and more, and still more, that's what they're asking for; that's how you'll hit the target of both profit and glory. Try to overwhelm your audience! Satisfying them is the real challenge.—What's wrong with you now? Is that pain, or pleasure, on your face?

POET. Go find yourself some more obedient slave! What—should the poet throw away, just to fatten your takings, the very thing that nature gave him, his highest right, the supreme claim of being human? How does he hold his free command over the human heart? How does he conquer the elements of life? Isn't it the harmony of his own heart, reaching outward far and wide, that draws the world into unison with him? When Nature's careless hand spins the endless thread on her spindle out into infinite distance, and the discordant tones of all existence clash together in a sullen jangle—who is it that divides the unchanging orders of creation and kindles them into rhythmic dance? Who brings the single note into the general harmony, so that it can throb in the grandest unison? Who commands the storm to stir passion in the human breast? Who makes the sunset burn above brooding souls? Who scatters every loveliest April blossom along love's shining path? Who weaves the plain, unremarkable leaves into crowns, rewarding merit in every field of action? Who secures Olympus and unites the gods there? The power of Man, as it is revealed in the poet.

MERRY-ANDREW. Well then, put all these fine powers together, and they'd drive the high business of poetry the same way they'd play out a love affair! You meet by chance, you feel something, you linger, and bit by bit your heart gets tangled up; happiness builds, and then it all gets thrown into confusion—you're swept away completely, then a touch of misery follows, and there's a neat little romance, wrapped up before you even know it happened! So let's give the audience exactly that kind of drama! Grab hold of the inexhaustible life that everyone actually lives! Everyone has a share in it, even if few really understand it—wherever you touch it, there's endless interest to be found. In brightly mixed pictures, not much clarity, plenty of error, and just a glimmer of truth—that's how the best brew gets made, the one that cheers and improves the whole world. Then, at your play, you'll see the finest flower of youth gathered to hear what you reveal! Every tender soul, with all its sentimental power, drinks in the melancholy nourishment your creation offers; and the leaven works now in this person, now in that one, because each person sees in it what's already lurking in his own chest. They're moved at once to tears or to laughter, still marvel at your flights of fancy, still enjoy the spectacle you put before them. A fully formed mind is never satisfied afterward; one still growing will always be grateful.

POET. Then give me back that season of pleasure, when I was still singing in joyous growth—when the crowding verses gushed and leapt from me like an unbroken fountain! Back then a bright mist veiled the world before me, and every opening bud seemed a marvel as I plucked the thousand blossoms that filled every valley for me! I had nothing, and yet I had enough for a young man—joy in illusion, a burning thirst for truth. Give me back, without restraint, that old emotion, that happiness that verged on pain, that strength of hatred, that depth of love—oh, give me back my youth again!

MERRY ANDREW. Youth, my good friend, is certainly something you need—when enemies are pressing hard on you in a fight; when lovely girls, full of eager longing, hang on your chest and caress you; when the wreath beckons from the finish line of a hard-won race; when, after dancing yourself breathless, you spend the whole night carrying on. But to play that familiar harp yourself with real feeling, with grace and bold expression, and to walk toward a goal you've set for yourself, taking plenty of sweet detours along the way—that, my venerable friend, belongs to you, and we respect you no less for it. They say age makes people childish, but that's not true—we're only genuinely children still, in the season of old age!

MANAGER. You've traded enough words between you—what I want now is to see some results. While you're busy exchanging compliments, you could be doing something more useful. What's the point of talking about inspiration? It doesn't wait around for delay. If poetry is really your calling, then let poetry obey your will! You both know perfectly well what's missing here: the crowd is thirsting for the strongest brew, and I want you to get it brewing right away. What isn't done today won't get done tomorrow either. Don't waste a single day on pointless detours—seize every possible impression with bold, confident resolve, and make it firmly your own; then you'll keep working, because you'll have to. On our German stage, as you well know, everyone tries his hand at whatever he likes; so help yourself freely to props and scenery, and be sure to show off everything you can find! Use both the great and the lesser lights of heaven—squander the stars by the dozen if you like, throw in animals, birds, trees, rocks, and every other kind of prop, fire, water, darkness, day and night! In our cramped little theater, the whole circle of creation will appear this way, and move, exactly as we choose to drive it, from Heaven, across the World, and down into Hell!

chapters.title: Prologue in Heaven
paragraphs: [The Lord and the Heavenly Host; Mephistopheles enters later.]
[The three archangels step forward.]

RAPHAEL. The sun sings out, in rivalry with its brother spheres, its ancient circuit, and completes its preordained path through creation with a tread like thunder. The angels draw strength from the sight of it, though its splendor is beyond measure; the lofty works, though never fully understood, remain as radiant as on the very first day.

GABRIEL. And swift, faster than thought can follow, the splendor of the world spins around, its Eden-brightness of day forever giving way to the deep and terrible dark of night. The ocean's tides break in foam against the rocks' deep foundations, and both, caught up in the sphere's endless race, go whirling onward, eternal and swift!

MICHAEL. And rival storms rage abroad, from sea to land and land to sea, forging round everything a chain of deepest violence in furious energy. There a flash of devastation blazes ahead of the crashing thunder—yet, Lord, your messengers still praise the gentle unfolding of your day.

ALL THREE. Though it remains beyond their understanding, the angels draw their strength from these very works, and all your creations, sublime and splendid, remain as radiant as at the hour of creation.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Since you, Lord, deign to come near again and ask, so kindly, how we're all doing, and since you used to enjoy meeting me yourself, here I am again, among your servants. Forgive me—I can't keep up with this crowd's lofty speeches, even though they scorn and mock me for it. My kind of feeling would surely make you laugh, if you hadn't forgotten how to laugh altogether. I've got nothing to report about suns and worlds—all I've noticed is how badly people torment themselves. That little god of the world still carries on in the same old way, still as odd as he was on the day of creation. He might actually be a bit better off, if you hadn't lent him that spark of heavenly light. He calls it Reason, and all it's done is make him more thoroughly bestial than any beast. If I may say so in your gracious presence, he strikes me as nothing more than one of those long-legged grasshoppers that leap up and fly, then fly and leap again, singing that same old tune in the grass. I'd almost prefer he stayed lying in the grass he came from—but no, he has to go sticking his nose into every pile of dung he finds.
THE LORD. Is that all you have to report? Do you always come only to find fault? Can you never find anything right on earth, ever?
MEPHISTOPHELES. No, Lord! Down there things are still as bad as ever. Even I feel a kind of pity watching men suffer—I hardly have the heart to torment the poor wretches any further.
THE LORD. Do you know Faust?
MEPHISTOPHELES. The one they call Doctor Faust?
THE LORD. My servant, yes.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Indeed! He serves you in a strange way, though. No earthly food or drink satisfies the fool. His spirit's restlessness drives him far beyond himself; half aware of his own frenzied, maddened unrest, he demands the fairest stars out of heaven, and from earth he demands the highest raptures and the best there is, and nothing near or far that he desires can ever calm the turmoil in his chest.

THE LORD. However confused his service to me may seem now, I will soon lead him into clearer daylight. Doesn't a gardener know, even while a tree is still budding, that flower and fruit will grace it in the years to come?
MEPHISTOPHELES. What will you wager? You could still lose him—if you'll give me full permission to lead him gently down my own road!
THE LORD. As long as he lives on earth, I place no prohibition on you. While a man's desires and strivings are still in motion, he can't help but go astray.

MEPHISTOPHELES. My thanks! I've never had much use for the dead, and never cared to keep them around. I much prefer cheeks still flushed with living blood, and when a corpse comes near, I shut my door—it's the same as a cat with a mouse.

THE LORD. Enough! What you've asked is granted. Lead this spirit away from his true source; catch him in your snares, if you can, and drag him downward with you. But you'll stand ashamed in the end, forced to admit: a good man, even lost in the dark and struggling toward something he can barely name, still keeps some instinct for the one true path.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Agreed! It won't take long, in any case. I have no worries at all about this wager. If I succeed the way I expect to, you'll let me celebrate my triumph with a swelling chest. He'll eat dust, and relish it, the way my old relation the serpent did.

THE LORD. In that, you're free to do as you see fit—I've never held your kind in hatred. Of all the spirits who deny and defy, the mischievous rogue causes me the least trouble. Man's active nature tends to slacken too soon and slide into wanting nothing but rest; that's exactly why I've gladly given him a companion who stirs him up, provokes him, and has to keep creating, in his role as Devil. But you, the sons of God, rejoice in the rich, ever-living beauty around you! Let the creative power that works its eternal designs hold you fast in bonds of love that never loosen, and take whatever flickers and wavers into being and fix it firmly in place with thoughts that stand forever!
[Heaven closes; the archangels go their separate ways.]

MEPHISTOPHELES (alone). I do enjoy, now and then, hearing the Old One talk, and I'm careful to stay on civil terms with him. It really is decent of such a distinguished Lord to chat so humanly, even with the Devil!

chapters.title: Night
paragraphs: [A high-vaulted, cramped, Gothic room. FAUST sits restless in a chair at his desk.]

FAUST. I've now studied philosophy, law, and medicine—and, God help me, theology too—all the way through, with fierce effort. And here I stand, poor fool, no wiser than before, for all my learning. I'm called Master, even Doctor, and for ten years now, straight or crooked, rightly or wrongly, I've led my students around by the nose—only to see that nothing can really be known! That realization cuts me to the bone. I'm cleverer, true enough, than all those foppish doctors, masters, scribes, and preachers; no scruples or doubts trouble me any longer, and neither Hell nor the Devil can frighten me anymore. But because of all this I've given up every pleasure; I don't pretend to know anything worth knowing, I don't pretend I could teach anyone or help or convert a single soul. On top of that, I have neither land nor gold, not the smallest scrap of the world's pomp or honor—no dog would put up with such a wretched existence! That's why I've turned to magic for help, hoping that through the power and speech of spirits I might reach many a secret, and so be spared the bitter task of speaking about things I don't actually know. I want to grasp the innermost force that holds the world together and drives it forward, to explore its seeds and its creative powers, and stop rummaging around in empty words. Oh full and radiant moon, whom I've watched climb the sky from this desk so many midnights—if only your light were shining on my misery for the last time! Your eye, my most mournful friend, has always found me bent over books and papers; but how I wish that I could stand instead on some great mountain in your blessed glow, hover with spirits through mountain caverns, drift with you in twilight across the meadows, and, freed from the fog of learning that wraps around me, bathe myself back to health in your dewy springs! Ah, but instead I still see this dungeon, this dreary, cursed pile of masonry, where even the welcome daylight only manages to filter dimly through the stained glass panes. Hemmed in by tottering heaps of worm-eaten books, gray with dust, that climb clear to the vaulted ceiling, pressed against smoke-stained paper; surrounded by glass jars and boxes stacked around me, instruments thrown together every which way, ancestral junk crammed in on every side—this is my world, and what a world it is! And do I still ask why my heart falters, weighed down by needs I can't even name? Why some inexplicable ache blocks every movement of my life? Ah, instead of the living Nature in which God set his human creature, I'm surrounded still by smoke and mold, by fleshless dead things and the bones of beasts! Fly! Get up and seek the wide-open land! Isn't this one book of mysteries, in Nostradamus's own hand, company enough for me? Once I know the courses of the stars, once I seek out Nature's wise instruction, my soul will glow with real power, the way spirit speaks to spirit. It's useless, this empty brooding here, even if I manage to guess at the holy symbols. Spirits, come—you're hovering near—oh, if you can hear me, answer me! Ha! What sudden rapture leaps out at me from this sight, flowing swiftly through all my senses! I feel a youthful, holy, vital bliss glowing fresh in every vein and fiber. Was it some god who drew this sign, calming my turmoil, unsealing my troubled heart to joy, revealing to me, with a mystic and divine impulse, the powers of Nature all around my path? Am I myself a god? Everything looks so clear to me now! In these pure lines I see creative Nature unfolding before my soul. Now, for the first time, I understand what the old sage meant: 'The spirit world is never closed off; it's your senses that are shut, your heart that is dead. Rise, disciple, and tirelessly hurry to bathe your chest in the red light of morning!' See how each part gives its substance to the Whole, each working and living within the other! Like heavenly forces rising and descending, passing their golden vessels back and forth to one another, with wings that winnow blessing, I see them pressing down from Heaven through Earth, filling the whole of everything with unceasing harmony! What a magnificent sight—but ah, only a sight. Boundless Nature, how do I make you truly mine? Where are you, breasts? Shining founts of all being, on which the longing of Heaven and Earth both hang, toward which our withered hearts reach out—you flow, you nourish, and am I left pining here for nothing? How differently this sign affects me! You, Spirit of the Earth, are closer to me: already I feel my powers rising, growing clearer; I glow as if drunk on new wine. New strength and courage to face the world stir in me, the sorrow of earth and the joy of earth both call to me, and even if storms crash down on me, no shipwreck could ever frighten me! Clouds are gathering above me— the moon hides her light— the lamp goes out!— mists rise—red, angry flashes dart around my head!—A horror falls from the vaulted ceiling and seizes me! I feel your presence, spirit I've summoned! Show yourself! Ha, what a wrenching blow strikes my heart! My senses heave in a fresh convulsion! I feel you pulling at my heart, drawing me in, draining me dry: you must appear, you must—even if it costs me my life!
[He opens the book and sees the sign of the Macrocosm.]
[He gazes at the sign.]
[He flips the pages impatiently and sees the sign of the Earth-Spirit.]
[He grabs the book and speaks the spirit's sign in a hushed, mysterious voice. A reddish flame flares up; the Spirit appears within it.]
SPIRIT. Who is calling me?
FAUST (turning his face away). Terrible to look at!
SPIRIT. For a long time you've drawn me toward you with all your strength, for a long time you've demanded your nourishment from my sphere, and now—
FAUST. No! I can't bear the sight of you!

SPIRIT. To see me was your ambition, to hear my voice, to look upon my face; your powerful longing has moved me, and here I am! What is this turmoil that shakes you, you who claimed to be more than human? Where is that lofty calling of your soul now? Where is the breast that once bore a whole world within itself, that shaped and cherished it, that swelled with joy at the thought of standing as our equal, banded together with us spirits? Where are you, Faust, whose voice reached all the way to me, who pressed toward me with all your strength? Is this really you—trembling through every depth of your being at the mere breath and sight of my presence, a writhing worm, a form shrunk in terror?
FAUST. Should I fear you, a mere shape of flame? Yes—I am Faust, I am your equal!

SPIRIT. In the tides of life, in the storm of action, I am a wave that surges and falls, a shuttle flying free between birth and the grave, an eternal sea, a weaving, flowing life all aglow—so it is that at the humming loom of Time, my hand prepares the garment that the Godhead wears!
FAUST. You, who travel around the whole wide world, you tireless spirit—how close I feel to you!
SPIRIT. You're like the spirit that you can comprehend—not like me!
[Vanishes.]

FAUST (overwhelmed). Not like you! Then like whom? I, the very image of the Godhead! Not even your equal! Oh, death—I know it already—it's my assistant! My finest stroke of luck comes to nothing: right in the middle of my vision's full richness, that soulless creature has to come disturb me like this!
[A knock at the door.]
[WAGNER enters in a dressing-gown and nightcap, carrying a lamp. FAUST turns toward him, impatient.]

WAGNER. Forgive me, I heard you declaiming—surely you were reading some old Greek tragedy? I'd love a little training in that art myself, since it's useful to have these days. I've often heard it said that even a preacher could learn something from an actor as his teacher.
FAUST. Yes—when the preacher happens to be an actor by nature, as does occasionally happen.

WAGNER. Ah, but when a man studies the way I do, shut up like a prisoner, barely glimpsing the world even on holidays, and then only through a window pane, on rare occasions—how is he ever supposed to learn to sway people through persuasion?

FAUST. You'll never manage it unless you have the real feeling for it—unless it rises clear from your own soul, serene in its own native strength, compelling to the hearts and minds of everyone who hears it. Instead you sit forever gluing scraps together, patching things up, cooking up leftovers from other people's tables, and out of your heap of ashes you hatch some starveling flame and blow on it to keep it barely alive! Go ahead and win the admiring stares of children and monkeys, if that satisfies you—but you'll never speak from heart to heart in a way that truly inspires, unless your own heart is speaking with real eloquence.
WAGNER. And yet it's through delivery that orators succeed; I do feel I'm still far behind in that, it's true.

FAUST. Look for honest reward instead! Watch out you don't turn into some tinkling fool! Clear wit and real sense, even with little artifice, will find their own way of expressing themselves—and if you're genuinely moved to speak, what need do you have to go chasing after fine words? Your speeches, for all their glittering show, where you twist shredded thoughts into shapes like paper cutouts for people, are as unrefreshing as the winds that blow rustling leaves through the cold autumn mist!

WAGNER. Ah, God, but Art is long, and life, alas, is short. And often, working hard at my critical duties, I feel something's wrong, in both my head and my chest. How hard it is to lay hold of the means by which one rises all the way to the source! And it may be that, before a man has traveled even half the road, the poor devil has to quit this life altogether.

FAUST. Is parchment, then, the sacred spring in front of you, a drink that will quench your thirst forever? No true refreshment can restore you except what breaks forth spontaneously from your own soul.

WAGNER. Forgive me, but it's a great delight, once you've planted yourself in the spirit of past ages, to trace how some sage thought before our time, and then to see how far, and how grandly, we've carried his work forward since.

FAUST. Oh yes, all the way to the stars, no doubt! Listen, my friend: the past ages are a book sealed with seven seals now. What you call the Spirit of the Ages is really nothing but the spirit of you scholars yourselves, in which those ages happen to be reflected. So more often than not you make a miserable mess of it! Anyone who takes a first real look runs away—it looks like a garbage barrel, a junk-filled attic, or at best a Punch-and-Judy show, full of glib, hard-hitting maxims exactly suited to the mouths of puppets!
WAGNER. But still—the world, the human heart and mind! Surely one can be forgiven for wanting at least some small understanding of those.

FAUST. Yes, the kind of understanding that men actually manage to reach! Who dares call the child by its true name in public? The few who ever really learned anything of the sort, unwisely frank, their hearts refusing to hide it, laid bare every thought and feeling to the mob—and they've been crucified and burned for it, every time. I beg you, my friend, it's the dead of night now; we'll have to break off our conversation here.

WAGNER. I would gladly have kept watch with you all night, so our learned talk could go on longer. But tomorrow, in the Easter holiday, I'll ask you this and that question, whenever it suits you. I pursue learning most zealously—I already know a great deal, but my ambition is to know everything.
[He leaves.]

FAUST (alone). Only a mind that chooses to stick forever in shallow rubbish never loses hope—the kind that digs eagerly for buried treasure and rejoices when it turns up nothing but an earthworm! Could a human voice like that dare interrupt the fullest flow of spirit-presence all around me here? And yet, just this once, I owe you my thanks—you, the poorest, dullest of all earth's sons! Because you tore me away from a desperate state that was about to overwhelm my senses completely: the apparition was so gigantic that it dwarfed and withered every pretension my soul ever had. I, the image of God, who began to believe eternal truth lay within my easy reach, who set out to sun myself in heavenly light and clarity, and cast off the merely earthly man—I, greater than any cherub, whose free power had planned to flow through Nature's veins in joyful pulsation, to reach beyond and enjoy, as the gods do, the very life of creation—look now at my punishment! One word of thunder has swept me from where I stood. I don't dare compare myself to you. Though I had the power to draw you near me, the power to hold onto you was denied my hand. In that ecstatic moment I felt myself both so small and so great; but you've ruthlessly thrust me back onto man's uncertain fate. What should I avoid? Whose guidance should I follow? Should I simply accept all this stress and struggle? Ah, every deed we do, no less than every sorrow we suffer, only slows down the onward march of life. Some foreign, alien substance keeps clinging more and more to everything the mind imagines as grand and beautiful; and once we've actually achieved this world's version of the Good, the Better gets branded a cheat and a trap. The fine feelings out of which we shape our lives lie mute and cold once caught in the world's turmoil. If hopeful imagination once spread her longing out in daring flight toward the Infinite, now she's content with a much narrower space, since Time's wild waves have stranded so many a fortune along the way. Care lurks at the very bottom of the heart, working her secret pangs in silence, rocking herself restlessly, disturbing both joy and rest; she's always dressed in some new mask, appearing now as house and land, now as wife and child, now as water, fire, poison, or steel. We dread blows that never actually strike us, and we mourn even for things we never actually lose! I'm not like the Gods! I feel that truth far too deeply. I'm the worm that crawls in the dust, that, even while it lives in the dust and searches for its bread, gets crushed and buried under some wanderer's footstep. Isn't this dust exactly what these walls hold in—these hundred shelves that cramp and chain me in, this thousandfold clutter of trinkets and rubbish that hems me into this moth-eaten den? Is this really where I'll find the help I need? Are a thousand volumes here only going to teach me that men everywhere torture themselves and bleed, and that here and there some one lonely man sits happy? What do you mean by that grin, you hollow skull—except that your brain, like mine, was once a cloudy mirror that sought the bright light of day, and then, in a dull twilight, thirsting for truth, wandered wretchedly into error? You instruments, indeed, do nothing but mock me with your wheels and gears and strange, clumsy shapes of wonder; I found the door, and you were supposed to be the keys—your wards are cleverly cut, but you drive no bolts open! Even in broad daylight Nature stays mysterious, keeping her veil on no matter how loudly we protest; whatever she doesn't willingly show us can't be wrenched from her with levers, screws, and hammers. You ancient tools, whose purpose I never even learned, you've been moldering here since my father used you; and you, ancient scroll, have worn that smoky color ever since the dim lamp used to smolder at this same desk. It would have been far better, I confess, if I'd simply spent my little inheritance freely rather than sweating now beneath its weight! Whatever is lent to you from your fathers' legacy, you must earn all over again, if you really want to possess it. Whatever serves no purpose is only a painful burden: it's the need of the moment that creates the thing meant to serve and bless it! But why does my gaze turn so readily toward that one spot? Is that flask over there acting like a magnet on my eyes? Why does the air all around me suddenly glow so brightly, the way soft moonlight lies over a nighttime forest? I greet you, wondrous, rarest little vial! I take you down reverently, ready for the trial: I honor human skill and craft in you. You, summary of gentle sleep-inducing draughts, essence of the finest and deadliest powers and uses, show your master your favor freely now! The moment I look at you, the stings of pain grow fainter; the moment I hold you, my struggles slowly come to an end: the flood-tide of my spirit ebbs away more and more. My dreaming speeds out onto the open ocean; the glassy water gleams before my feet, and a new day beckons toward a newer shore! A fiery chariot, carried on buoyant wings, sweeps toward me now! I'll soon be ready to pierce through ether's high, unknown domains, to reach new spheres of pure activity! Do I, who was only a worm a moment ago, deserve to pursue this godlike rapture, this supreme existence? Yes—resolute to reach some brighter distance, I turn my back on the fair sun of Earth. Yes, let me dare to fling open those gates that every man would rather slink quietly past! It's time to thunder out this truth through action: that man's dignity can rival the very height of the gods! Nor should I shrink back frightened from that gloomy gulf, where imagination torments itself with pangs of its own making—to struggle instead toward that darkened passage, around whose narrow mouth all the fires of Hell are burning—to take this step with cheerful resolve, even if utter nothingness turns out to be the swift and certain outcome! And now come down, you clearest crystal cup! You emerge fresh from your ancient case, forgotten by my mind for so many years! You used to shine at cheerful old family banquets, making the solemn guests merry as one passed your toast on to the next. My memory, from many a night of youth, still holds those rich, skillfully carved figures worked into your surface, and the drinker's duty—explained in rhyme—of draining you in one breath down to some mark or other. Now I'll never pass you to a neighbor again, nor try to match my wit against your curious craftsmanship. Here instead is a liquid from which sleep is swiftly born. It fills your crystal hollow with a darker flood; I chose it, I prepared it myself: so now I follow through—with all my soul I swallow this final drink, a solemn festive toast, a greeting to the morning! [He raises the goblet to his lips. Bells chime, and a chorus begins to sing.] CHORUS OF ANGELS. Christ has risen! Joy to the mortal soul, once imprisoned by inherited needs that clung to him though he never earned them. FAUST. What is this hollow humming, this sharp, clear tone that pulls the goblet from my lips just as they were about to meet? Are those booming bells already announcing the first glad hour of Easter's festival? Choirs, have you already begun that sweet, consoling chant that the ministering angels once sang through the night of death, proclaiming God's new covenant?

CHORUS OF WOMEN. With spices and precious balm we anointed him; faithful and tender, we laid him gently to rest; we wound clean linen around him to bind him. Ah, but when we came looking for him, we found no Christ there anymore!
CHORUS OF ANGELS. Christ has ascended! Bliss now clothes him—every sorrow that afflicted him, every trial that tested him, has come to a glorious end!

FAUST. Why do you cast your spell on me here in the dust, you gentle, powerful sounds of Heaven? Ring out instead where tender souls still dwell. I hear your message, but I haven't been given the faith for it; and the dearest child of Faith is Miracle. I don't dare soar up to those regions from which the glad tidings come floating down; and yet, familiar with that note since childhood, it renews in me now my old allegiance to life. Once, Heavenly Love sent down a burning kiss upon my forehead, in the holy silence of the Sabbath; and, full of some mystic foreboding, the church bell chimed slowly, and prayer dissolved me into fervent bliss. A sweet, incomprehensible yearning drove my feet out through the free woods and meadows, and while a thousand tears burned in me, I felt a whole world rising up for me. These chants, which once appealed to youth and all its games, proclaimed the joyful holiday of spring; and now memory, with a child's feeling, holds me back from taking that last, solemn step. Sound on, hymns of Heaven, so sweet and gentle! My tears gush forth: the Earth takes her child back!

CHORUS OF DISCIPLES. Has he truly burst victorious from the vaulted grave, and now sits exalted in glory? Is he near, radiant with the glow of new birth, in creative rapture? Ah, we still belong here, native to earth's sorrow. We, his eager followers, miss him; weeping, we long for it, Master—your bliss!

CHORUS OF ANGELS. Christ is risen, out of the womb of corruption: burst your own prison, break free from your gloom! Praise him and plead with him, love him and need him, feed one another as brothers, preach him and speed him onward, bless him and carry his work forward—this is how the Master stays near, this is how he is here!

chapters.title: Before the Gate
paragraphs: [All sorts of people come out walking.]
SEVERAL APPRENTICES. Why are you going that way?
OTHERS. We're headed to the Hunters' Lodge today.
THE FIRST. We're strolling down to the mill, in the hollow over there.
AN APPRENTICE. I'd say head for the River Tavern.
SECOND APPRENTICE. But that's not a pleasant walk, though.
THE OTHERS. And what will you do?
A THIRD. Wherever the crowd goes, I follow.
A FOURTH. Come up to Burgdorf, why don't you? You'll find good cheer there, the finest girls and the best beer, and plenty of rowdy brawling too, trust me!
A FIFTH. You swaggering fool, is your hide itching for a third beating already? I won't go there—your idea of a good brawl disgusts me!
SERVANT-GIRL. No, no—I'm turning around and going back to town.
ANOTHER. We'll be sure to find him over by those poplars.
THE FIRST. That's no great luck for me, clearly. You'll have him wherever and whenever you go—you'll be his dance partner—but what good is your fun to me?
THE OTHER. He surely won't be alone today—I heard he'll have Curly-head with him.

A STUDENT. Look at those buxom girls step along! Come on, brother, we've got to walk them to their seats. A strong old beer, a pipe that bites and stings, a girl in her Sunday best—those three are all the delight I need.
CITIZEN'S DAUGHTER. Just look at those handsome fellows over there! It's really a shame, I must say—chasing after servant girls, when they could have the most refined company today, if they wanted!

SECOND STUDENT (to the First). Not so fast! Two others are coming up behind—those two dressed so neatly and prettily. One of them is my neighbor, and she's completely won my heart. They walk along so demurely, but I'm sure they'll accept us in the end.
THE FIRST. No, brother—their prim manners aren't for me. Quick, before our game slips away in the crowd: the hand that wields the broom on Saturday will do the best fondling and caressing on Sunday.

CITIZEN. He doesn't suit me at all, our brand-new Burgomaster! Ever since he took office, he's grown more and more arrogant. How has he helped the town, I ask you? Things just keep getting worse—what improvement can he point to? He demands more obedience from us than ever, and we pay more than ever, too!

BEGGAR (sings). Good gentlemen and lovely ladies, so rosy-cheeked and finely dressed, look how badly I need your help here, take a look and lighten my distress! Don't let me sing my song in vain—only the man who gives away is glad. Let this holiday, which shows off your pity, become a harvest-day for me!

ANOTHER CITIZEN. On Sundays and holidays, there's nothing I enjoy more than gossiping about war and its doings, when far off in Turkey the foreign peoples are busy fighting each other. One sits at the window with a glass and friends, watching all sorts of ships glide down the river, and then, heading home at night, gives thanks for the peaceful times we live in.

THIRD CITIZEN. Yes, neighbor, that's exactly how I feel too. Let them break each other's heads and let their passions loose, and let everything over there get mixed up in chaos—so long as here, we keep our good old ways!

OLD WOMAN (to the Citizen's Daughter). Dear me, how fine you look! So handsome, and so young! Who wouldn't lose his heart to you? Don't be so proud, now—I'll keep quiet, and whatever it is you'd like, I'll see to it that you get it.

CITIZEN'S DAUGHTER. Come along, Agatha—I'd rather avoid being seen with that witch in public, people might get the wrong idea. It's true, though, she showed me on Saint Andrew's Night my future sweetheart, just as clear as if he were standing right there.
THE OTHER. She showed me mine too, in clear crystal, several wild young fellows, and a soldier as my lover. I look for him everywhere, I search and search, but somehow I can never find his face.

SOLDIERS. Castles with lofty ramparts and towers, proud maidens dressed in all their beauty—both shall be ours! Bold is the venture, splendid the pay! Lads, let the trumpets sound the call for us, summoning us to pleasure, summoning us to ruin. Our life is a stormy one; that's its whole reward! Maidens and castles both surrender soon enough. Bold is the venture, splendid the pay! And the soldiers go marching, marching away!
[Faust and Wagner enter.]

FAUST. Brook and river are freed from ice by the quickening gaze of gracious spring; the colors of hope cling to the valley now, and weak old Winter himself has to retreat, shivering, up into the mountains, a king without his crown. From up there, as he keeps retreating, he still sends down feeble showers of sleet that streak the green plain in dark bands. But the sun won't allow any white to linger; everywhere form is developing and growing—he'll brighten the world with the colors he loves, and since there aren't yet real flowers, blue, yellow, and red, he makes do with these gaudy crowds of people instead. Turn around now, and look back at the town from up here on this rise. Out of the dark, hollow gate the motley crowds come pouring, full of joy. Everyone wants to hoard their share of sunshine today, to honor the day the Lord rose from the dead! They feel their own resurrection in it too—out of their low, dark, barely livable rooms; free of the bonds of work and the constraints of trade; free of the crushing weight of roofs and gables; out of the narrow, choking streets and alleys; out of the solemn, reverent dark of the churches—all of them come out into the cheerful light. Look how lively the crowd streams out, scattering through gardens and distant fields, while out on the broadly rippling river so many festive boats go dancing by; and, loaded almost to sinking, the last full ferry pushes off downstream. Even far off, on the hillside paths, their clothes gleam in soft patches of color. I can hear the noise of the village itself. This is the people's real heaven; here both high and low are content to see each other! Here I am a man—here I dare to be one!

WAGNER. Strolling with you, Doctor, is flattering—both an honor and a benefit to me. But on my own, I'd avoid these shallow pastimes, since everything coarse offends me. I hate this fiddling, shouting, bowling, all this noise of the crowd: they carry on as though the Devil himself were running their games, and they call it merriment, call it song!

PEASANTS, UNDER THE LINDEN TREE (dancing and singing). The shepherd dressed himself up for the dance, in ribbons, a wreath, and his gayest vest, taking great care over his appearance. Around the linden tree, the lads and lasses were already stepping it out like mad: hurrah, hurrah, hurrah, tarara-la, while the fiddle-bow played on. He broke through the ranks without a bit of fear, and elbowed a girl who stood watching the dance. The buxom girl turned and said, 'Now that's what I call a stupid-head!' Hurrah, hurrah, hurrah, tarara-la—'behave decently while you're here!' Then round the circle they went flying, dancing left, dancing right, their skirts all swinging along. They grew red-faced first, then grew warm, and rested, panting, arm in arm—hurrah, hurrah, hurrah, tarara-la—hips and elbows wandering freely. Now don't get so familiar here! Plenty of a girl's been fooled that way, led astray and betrayed! And yet he coaxed her aside all the same, and the sound rang wide around the linden tree. Hurrah, hurrah, hurrah, tarara-la, and the fiddle-bow kept playing.

OLD PEASANT. It's very good of you, Doctor, to come down among us and mingle today, a highly learned man among this crowd of ordinary, merry folk. Here, take this finest mug too—we've filled it with fresh wine, just for you. I offer it to you and humbly hope that it doesn't just quench your thirst, but that for every drop that sinks below its rim, you'll be granted just as many more days of life!
FAUST. I accept the cup you so kindly offer, with thanks, and I drink to the health of every one of you.
[The people gather around him in a circle.]

OLD PEASANT. Truly, it's fitting and well-timed that you share our day of joy with us today, you who in harder times gave us so much of your care and help. Many a man still stands here alive because your father's skillful hand snatched him from the fever's grip and held the plague back across the whole land. And you too, though you were still young then, went into every house of sickness; many corpses were carried out, but you always came out again in good health.
FAUST. You never shrank from any test or trial. A helping God assisted the one who helped.
ALL. Health to the man, so skilled and so well-tested—may he live on long, still helping us!
FAUST. Bow down instead to Him above, my friends, who teaches us to help and sends us aid!
[He walks on with Wagner.]

WAGNER. What a feeling it must be for you, great man, to receive such honest veneration from these people! How fortunate is the one whose gifts bring him such advantages from his own position! The fathers point you out to their children; everyone asks about you and crowds close to look; the fiddle stops, the dance pauses. You walk by, and they line up in rows to watch, all caps lifted high—another moment and they'd practically kneel, as if the Holy Sacrament itself were passing by.

FAUST. Let's climb a few more steps, as far as that stone over there—there we'll rest from our wandering, content. I've often lingered here alone, lost in thought, back when foolish fasting and prayer tormented my life. Here, rich in hope and firm in faith, with tears, wringing my hands and sighing, I struggled and begged the Lord of Heaven to bring an end to that far-reaching plague of death! Now the crowd's applause feels almost like contempt to me. If only you could read what's in my innermost spirit, you'd see how little I now believe that either my father or I deserve such praise! My father had a somber, brooding mind, which groped and wandered through Nature's sacred realms, and honestly pondered things in his own peculiar way, with strange and painful effort. Shut up in his dim workshop with a circle of proven fellow-adepts, he brewed endless recipes to force opposing substances to combine. There was a 'red lion,' a bold suitor, married off in the tepid bath of the 'lily,' and both of them, tormented by relentless flame, were then moved back and forth between one bridal chamber and the other. If the 'young queen' then appeared in splendid colors inside her glass vessel, that was the medicine—the patients' suffering soon ended, and nobody ever asked who actually got well. So we, mixing our hellish pills, passed through these valleys and hills worse than the plague itself. I gave poison that killed thousands, and now I have to listen to the living praise us as though we were anything but shameless murderers!

WAGNER. Why let yourself sink into such gloom over it? A good man does his honest part simply by practicing, with the utmost care, the art that's been handed down to him! If you honor your father as a young man, then let his teaching cheerfully spur you on; and if, as a grown man, you add to the store of human knowledge, then your own son may go on to surpass you in turn.

FAUST. Happy the man who can still renew the hope of rising forever out of the depths of error! What one doesn't know is exactly what one needs, and what one does know, one never gets to use. But let's not sour the good fortune of this hour with such gloomy thoughts! Look how the green-embosomed houses glitter under the glow of the evening sun! The sun is retreating, the day's work is done; it hurries off now to explore new fields of life elsewhere. Ah, if only some wing could lift me from the ground, to follow it, follow it, soaring on its track! Then I would watch it gild the silent world below me in an endless evening, every mountain peak on fire, every valley filled with peace, the silver brook flowing into rivers of gold. The mountain range, with all its deep gorges, would no longer block my godlike motion, and already the ocean opens before my eyes, with all its bays, lying in shining sleep! And yet, in the end, the weary god sinks down; but a new impulse fires my mind at once—I hurry on, drinking in his eternal rays, the day ahead of me, the night behind, the sky unfurled above me, the floor of waves beneath—a glorious dream, though its glories are already fading. Alas, no wings that lift the mind can lend any wings to lift the body along with it. And yet it's born in every soul, this pleasure of yearning onward, upward, and away, whenever, high overhead, lost in the vaulted blue, the lark sends down his flickering song—whenever, over crags and pine-covered heights, the eagle hovers, slowly soaring—and whenever, over plains and lakes and islands, the crane sails onward toward other shores.

WAGNER. I've had my own odd whims at times, but never anything quite like that impulse. One tires quickly enough of staring at woods and fields, and I'd never envy the bird his wing. How differently the pleasures of the mind carry us instead, from page to page, from book to book! Winter nights take on an untold loveliness that way, as if warm new life had crowned every limb of you; and when your hands unroll some rare old parchment, all of Heaven comes down and opens up bright around you!

FAUST. You're only aware, at best, of one of these impulses—never try to learn about the other! Two souls live within my breast, alas, and each one pulls away from, and fights against, the other. One of them clings to the world with all its might, holding on with organs of lust and love; the other tears itself violently up out of the dust, into the high realms of our ancestors. If there really are spirits in the air, ruling in the space between Heaven and Earth, let them descend out of that golden atmosphere and carry me off into new and richer life! Yes, if I only owned a magic cloak to carry me wherever I pleased across the world, I wouldn't trade it—not for the richest treasure, not for a king's own robe!

WAGNER. Don't call up that all-too-familiar crowd like that—the ones drifting through the sky, preparing a thousandfold danger for our kind, arriving from every direction. Sharp spirit-fangs sweep down swiftly from the North and attack you with their barbed points; then from the East they come to dry out and shrivel your lungs until your very breath fails you; if the South sends them out of the desert, they pile fire on top of the fire already burning your forehead; and the West leads on a horde that only 'cures' the drought by drowning meadow, field, and you along with it. They listen gladly, always ready to do harm—gladly obey, because deceiving us delights them; they pretend to come from Heaven, and lisp like angels even while they're lying to your face. But come, let's go—everything's turning gray and dim now. The air's grown cold, the mist is settling. It's at night that a man learns to value his own house. Why are you standing there with such astonished eyes? What in this twilight has your mind so troubled?
FAUST. Do you see that black dog running there, through the grain and the stubble?
WAGNER. I noticed him a while ago, but didn't think he was worth mentioning.
FAUST. Look at him closely—what do you take the creature for?
WAGNER. Why, for a poodle who's lost his master and is sniffing around trying to find his trail.

FAUST. Do you see the spiral circles, drawing in tighter, that he seems to be winding around us as he gets closer? Unless my eyes deceive me, a streaming trail of fire follows behind him on his mysterious path.
WAGNER. Your eyes may be deceiving you a little there; I see nothing but a plain black poodle.
FAUST. It seems to me he's using some enchanted cunning to snare our feet, meaning to bind us in some chain later on.
WAGNER. I just see him running around us timidly, uncertain, since he's found two strangers instead of his master.
FAUST. The circle's narrowing—he's close now!
WAGNER. What you're seeing here is a dog, not some phantom! Look, he's stopped—he's crawling on his belly, wagging his tail—all perfectly ordinary dog behavior!
FAUST. Come, follow us! Come here, at any rate!

WAGNER. He's the most absurd, comical creature. Stand still, and you'll see him wait patiently; speak to him, and he'll frisk about right away; if something's lost, he'll fetch it quickly enough—even your cane, if you toss it in the stream.
FAUST. No doubt you're right; I'll admit there's not a trace of mind in the beast—all I see is training, nothing more.
WAGNER. A well-trained dog is welcomed even by the wisest of men. Yes, he thoroughly deserves your favor—he's the star pupil among students, that one!
[They pass in through the city gate.]

chapters.title: The Study, Part 1
paragraphs: [Faust enters, with the poodle.]

FAUST. Behind me I leave field and meadow, sleeping now in a deep and prophetic night, within whose dread and holy keeping the better soul wakes into light. Wild desires no longer have any hold on us, deeds of passion no longer chain us; love of Man revives within us, and love of God revives again too. Quiet, poodle—don't make such a racket and commotion! Why are you sniffing so hard at the threshold? Go settle down quietly behind the stove—I'll give you my softest cushion. Since you amused us up there on the mountain crest with all your running and leaping, I'll take you in now, a welcome, but a quiet, guest. Ah, when the lamp glows with its friendly light in our narrow room, every faded ember flares up again in the chest, and in the heart that knows itself. Then hope offers its sweet help once more, and reason takes up her voice again: a man longs to reach the very rivers of existence, the true founts of life. Don't growl, poodle! Against the sound now rising, the sacred tones embracing my soul, this animal noise is out of place. We're used to seeing how Man despises whatever he can't understand, and belittles the Good and the Beautiful, finding them hard to measure—will the dog growl his displeasure too, just like a man? But ah, I feel it, no matter how much stronger my will grows, contentment no longer flows out of my chest. Why must the stream run dry so soon and fail us, leaving a burning thirst to assail us all over again? I've endured so much testing over this very question! And yet this lack can still be supplied; we call on the Supernatural to guide us; we pine and thirst for Revelation, and nowhere is it sent more worthily, more nobly, than here, in our New Testament. I feel compelled to work out its true meaning—honestly, once and for all, to turn the hallowed original into my own beloved German. (He opens a volume and begins.) It is written: 'In the beginning was the Word.' Here I'm already stuck—who can help me now? The Word? I can't possibly rate it that highly; I have to translate it differently. If the Spirit is truly guiding me, then it should read: 'In the beginning was the Thought.' Let me weigh this first line completely, so my impatient pen doesn't rush ahead too fast. Is it really the Thought that acts, that creates? 'In the beginning was the Power,' I read instead. And yet, even as I write it, something warns me that I still haven't quite captured the sense. The Spirit helps me now—I see the light! 'In the beginning was the Act,' I write. If I have to share my room with you, poodle, stop that howling, please! Stop barking and bellowing! I won't put up with such a noisy, disruptive creature near me any longer. One of us, do you hear me, is going to have to leave, I'm afraid. I'm withdrawing your guest-right—the door is open, you're free to go. But what am I seeing in this creature now? Is that within the course of nature? Is it actually happening, or is it some trick of my imagination? How long and broad my poodle is growing! He's rising up, huge: no dog's shape could ever do that! What a phantom I've been harboring here! He looks like a hippopotamus now, with fiery eyes, teeth terrible to see. Oh, now I'm sure of you! For every one of your half-hellish brood, the Key of Solomon will do the trick.

SPIRITS (in the corridor). Someone's caught in there! Stay outside, don't follow him in! Like a fox in a snare, the old hell-lynx trembles in there. Be careful—look around! Hover back and forth, above and below, and he'll work his own way free. If your help can do him any good, don't hold it back—after all, he's done so much, without limit, for our own pleasure.

FAUST. First, to confront the beast, let the words of the Four be spoken: Salamander, blaze gloriously! Undine, ripple as commanded! Sylph, make yourself invisible! Gnome, get to work! Whoever doesn't understand what these elements mean, whoever doesn't see their properties and their power, will never master the spirits. Vanish into flaming ether, Salamander! Flow foaming together, Undine! Shine with meteor-brightness, Sylph! Bring help to hearth and home, Gnome! Incubus, incubus, step forward and finish this! Not one trace of the Four lurks in this creature. He lies there quietly, grinning in disdain: it seems I haven't hurt him yet. Now then, to strip away your disguise, hear me exorcise you! Are you, my cheerful friend, one of Hell's runaway strays? Look upon this sign, before which the very legions of Hell bow down! His hair is bristling now, and he's starting to swell. Base creature, do you hear me? Do you know and fear the One who has no origin, whose name can't be spoken, who pervades all of Heaven, and who has been pierced beyond all remedy? Still confined behind the stove, look—he's swelling up into an elephant! He fills the whole space, melting like mist, faster and faster. Enough—rise no higher! Lay yourself down at the Master's feet! You see now, my threats weren't empty: I'll scorch and sting you with holy fire! Don't wait to find out about the threefold dazzling flame! Don't wait to find out the strongest art my hands possess!
MEPHISTOPHELES (as the mist clears, stepping out from behind the stove, dressed as a traveling scholar). Why all this noise? What does my lord command?
FAUST. So this was the poodle's true core all along—a traveling scholar? Well, that's an amusing turn of events.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I bow before the learned gentleman—you've certainly made me sweat, I'll give you that!
FAUST. What is your name?
MEPHISTOPHELES. That seems like a small question for someone whose mind despises mere words so much—who, scorning every surface gleam, values only the depths of being.

FAUST. With gentlemen of your sort, the name itself is usually a test, since it tends to express your true nature. That's certainly clear enough in names like Beelzebub, Destroyer, Father of Lies. So who, then, are you?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Part of that power which is never understood—the one that always wills evil, and always ends up doing good.
FAUST. What hidden meaning lies inside that riddle?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I am the Spirit that always says no! And rightly so—everything that gets called forth out of the Void deserves to be destroyed again; it would have been better if nothing had ever been created at all. So everything you people rate as Sin—destruction, anything mixed up with Evil—that's my true element.
FAUST. You call yourself a part, yet you appear whole to me?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I'm only speaking the modest truth to you. If Man, that fool of a microcosm, can so often see himself as a whole, then I'm a part of the Part—once, long ago, I was All, back in primal Night—a part of the Darkness that first brought forth the Light, that haughty Light which now disputes the space and claims from Mother Night her ancient territory. And yet the struggle fails, because however it weaves itself, Light still stays chained to bodies: it flows out of bodies, it makes bodies beautiful, and by bodies its course gets blocked. So it won't take much longer, I hope, before Light dies right along with the bodies that die.
FAUST. Ah, now I see the plan you're pursuing: since you can't manage total ruin all at once, you've started small instead.

MEPHISTOPHELES. And truly, it hasn't amounted to much, when all's said and done. This Something that stands stubbornly resisting Nothing—this clumsy world—hasn't, in spite of everything I've attempted, been shaken or disturbed by me in any real way: after earthquake, storm, flood, or volcanic fire, sea and land settle right back down into quiet! And that damned stuff, the bestial human brood—what good does it do me to have that to play with? I've done away with so many of them! And yet fresher, newer blood keeps right on circulating. It drives me furious just to watch it: out of Water, Earth, and Air, a thousand germs keep breaking out and growing, in dry ground and wet, in warm weather and cold; and if I hadn't kept the element of Fire in reserve, why, honestly, I'd have nothing special of my own left to show for it at all!

FAUST. So, against the ever-active, eternal creative force, all you can raise, in cold disdain, is your infernal fist, clenched wickedly and all in vain! Better go looking for some other line of work, you strange son of Chaos!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, we'll think it over—you can hear more of my views next time I venture in. For now, might I take my leave?

FAUST. I don't see why you'd even need to ask. Even though we've only just met, you have my leave to visit again. The window's right here, the door's over there; and you can see the chimney too, if you prefer.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I must confess I can't wander out that way—one small obstacle is holding my steps back: the wizard's pentagram drawn there on your threshold.

FAUST. The pentagram is stopping you? Well, tell me then, you son of Hades—if that's blocking your way, how did you ever get in here in the first place? Could a spirit like you really be tricked so easily?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Take a closer look—the drawing isn't finished. The outer angle, as you can see, is left open; the lines don't quite meet there.
FAUST. Well—chance has actually gotten it right this time! So you're my prisoner now? It seems the trick has worked after all.
MEPHISTOPHELES. The poodle didn't notice a thing when he came bounding in after you; but things look different now: the Devil can't get back out.
FAUST. Try the open windowpane, then!
MEPHISTOPHELES. For devils and spectres, this is the law: wherever they've entered, that's also where they must leave. We're free to choose the first, but bound by the second.
FAUST. So even Hell keeps its own laws, does it? Good—then surely a binding contract could also be made with you gentlemen?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Everything that's promised will delight you purely—you won't find me driving a stingy bargain. But this isn't something to settle in a hurry; we'll talk the matter over soon. For now, I beg this one favor—permission to withdraw from my intrusion here.
FAUST. Stay just one moment longer—at least tell me some pleasant news before you go.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Release me now! I'll come again soon enough; then you can question and press me all you like.
FAUST. I never set any snares around you; you led yourself right into the net. Whoever traps the Devil should hold him fast! It won't be soon that he catches such a precious prize a second time.
MEPHISTOPHELES. If it pleases you, I'm also content to stay and serve you in some agreeable capacity—on the condition that I'm allowed to entertain you with some of my own arts.
FAUST. I'll gladly agree to that, so long as the diversion is a pleasant one.

MEPHISTOPHELES. My friend, without any exaggeration, you'll gain more to soothe your senses in this one hour than in a whole year of dull routine. What the delicate spirits will sing to you, the lovely pictures they'll bring before you, are more than just magic's empty show. Your sense of smell will be invited into bliss; your palate will be delighted with flavor; your very nerves of touch will glow with ecstasy! I'll spin the charm without any preparation at all—we're here together, so let's begin!

SPIRITS. Vanish, you darkening arches above him! Let the loveliest weather, born of the blue sky, break free above! Oh, if only the darkening clouds would part! Starlight sparkles now, and calmer, gentler suns ride high. Heaven's own children, bewildering in their beauty, drift and sway as they hover past; an endless longing follows after them. Their glowing garments, streaming out behind them, cover, as they pass, whole landscapes and arbors, where, in seclusion, lovers pledge themselves, lost in sweet illusion. Bower upon bower! Vines untouched by blight! Look—in a sudden shower, clustered grapes burst into new wine, or pour into rivers of foaming, flashing wine that dashes gemlike as it bounds down from the high places, spreading and surrounding blossoming headlands and emerald shorelines with crystalline pools, in happy embraces! And the winged creatures drink, and fly onward, ever flying sunward toward those enticing islands that beckon, dipping and rising, light upon the water! Listen to the inspiring sound of their singing! See the entrancing whirl of their dance! All of them in the air grow freer and more beautiful. Some of them climb boldly toward the highlands, others go sailing, circling the islands; others still are flying, all of them hurrying toward life—all reaching for that distant star of living rapture and love!

MEPHISTOPHELES. He's asleep! That's enough, you sprites! You've sung him truly into slumber with your airy song: for that performance, I'm in your debt. You're not yet the man who can catch the Devil and hold him! Wrap him in the fairest images of dreams, plunge him deep into seas of sweet illusion! But as for the threshold magic that trapped him here—for that, the Devil needs a rat's quick tooth. I won't waste time on any long invocation: here's one now, rustling in, that will soon set me free. The lord of rats and also of mice, of flies and bedbugs, frogs and lice, summons you here to the doorsill, to gnaw at the very spot where, with just a touch of oil, he's marked it for you. There—you come hopping right over to me! Now, to work at once! The very point that stopped me is right there, carved on the ledge. One more bite frees the door. So dream your dreams, Faust, until we meet again!
FAUST (waking up). Have I been so foully cheated again? Is nothing left of that lofty encounter with the spirit—only a dream that the Devil faked, and a poodle that ran off?

chapters.title: The Study, Part 2
paragraphs: [Faust. Mephistopheles.]
FAUST. A knock? Come in! My peace disturbed again?
MEPHISTOPHELES. It's me!
FAUST. Come in!
MEPHISTOPHELES. It has to be said three times.
FAUST. Come in, then!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now that's more like it. I think we'll get along well. To chase off your gloom, I've come dressed as a fine young nobleman—scarlet coat with gold trim, a cloak that shimmers like silk, a tall rooster feather in my hat, a long sharp sword for show or for a fight. And my advice, in short: put on the same kind of splendid clothes yourself, so that once you're free of this den, you can finally see what life is like.

FAUST. This earthly life would still torment me the same way no matter what I wore. I'm too old to play at passion, too young to be free of desire. What is there left in the world for me? Deny yourself—give it up—hold back! That's the endless refrain droning in everyone's ears, the hoarse song that never stops, our whole life through, hour after hour. I wake in the morning in real terror, right at the edge of bitter tears, to see another day dawn that won't keep even one of my hopes—not one. Every anticipation of joy gets whittled down by stubborn doubt, blocked by life's grinning masks from ever letting my mind finish its finest work. And then, when night falls, I lie down on my bed anxious, and even there no rest comes to me; instead some wild dream is sent to torment me. The god living in my chest can stir the depths within me, but he has no power to move anything outside me. So, weighed down by the burden of my days, I long for death, and life feels like a curse.
MEPHISTOPHELES. And yet death is never an entirely welcome guest.

FAUST. Oh, lucky the man who, in the flash of victory, binds the bloody laurel to his brow! Or who, after some wild, frenzied dance, finds himself in a girl's embracing arms! Oh, if only I had collapsed and died before that mighty spirit, swept away from life!
MEPHISTOPHELES. And yet, on that same night, somebody didn't drink a certain liquid.
FAUST. Ha—so eavesdropping is your pleasure, is it?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'm not all-knowing, but I do know a good deal.

FAUST. Even though a familiar sound pulled my thoughts back from torment, and sweet, clear echoes came, tricking me with a faith left over from childhood—still I now curse everything that lures and snares the soul with empty visions, that traps it in this cave of pain with dazzling deceptions and cherished delusions. Cursed, above all, be the high ambition by which the mind deceives itself! Cursed be the glare of illusion that forces itself on our finer senses! Cursed be the lying dream of name and fame and the laurel crown! Cursed be everything that flatters us as possession—wife and child, servant and plow! Cursed be Mammon, when he spurs us with treasure into restless action, and cursed when, to give us soft and easy leisure, he smooths our pillows for us! Cursed be the wine's transcendent sweetness, that highest gift of love! Cursed be hope, cursed be faith—that phantom—and cursed, most of all, be patience!

CHORUS OF SPIRITS (invisible). Woe! Woe! You have destroyed it, the beautiful world, with your powerful fist! It is smashed to ruin, shattered by a demigod's blow! We carry the scattered fragments away into the void, mourning the beauty now lost beyond repair. Mightier one, for the sons of men, build it again—more brightly, build it anew in your own heart! Let a new life begin, with clearer understanding, and let new songs of joy be sung to greet it!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Those are my little helpers, keeping me company. Listen to them—they're urging you, in their shrewd, old-fashioned way, toward action and passion! They want to draw you out of this lonely life that's drained you of blood and feeling, into the thick of the world's struggle. Stop nursing this grief that gnaws at your chest like a vulture! Even the worst company will show you that you're a man among men. Not that I mean to throw you in with the mob you despise—I'm nobody grand myself. But if you'll trust your steps through life to me, I'll guide you; I'll walk beside you gladly; I'll serve you at once and forever, doing my best, and if you're satisfied, I'll stay with you as your servant, even your slave.
FAUST. And what would I owe you in return for that?
MEPHISTOPHELES. There's plenty of time for that—you don't need to press the point now.

FAUST. No, no. The Devil is an egotist, and isn't the type to help someone else out of the goodness of his heart, for nothing. Tell me your terms plainly and clearly! A servant like you is dangerous to have around, I suspect.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'll be bound to you here, tireless, at your beck and call, obeying your every whim. Then, when we meet again on the other side, you'll do the same for me.

FAUST. The other side troubles me very little. Once you've smashed this world to pieces, the other one can take its place. My pleasures spring from right here on this earth; this sun looks down on my sorrows as it makes its rounds. Once I've parted from these things, let happen whatever will! I don't want to hear any more about whether, over there, we go on loving or hating, or whether in those spheres we imagine, a heaven and a hell await our souls.
MEPHISTOPHELES. In that case, you can certainly risk it. Come, bind yourself by a quick agreement, and you'll get to see my arts with delight: I'll give you what no man has ever seen.

FAUST. What could you possibly give me, poor devil? Has a human soul, in its highest striving, ever once been understood by the likes of you? Still—do you have food that never satisfies, restless red gold that runs through the fingers like quicksilver, a game no one ever really wins, a girl who, even lying on my chest, makes eyes at my neighbor, and honor's godlike glow, that flares for a moment and burns out? Show me fruit that rots before it can be picked, and trees that put out fresh leaves every day!

MEPHISTOPHELES. A request like that doesn't scare me at all—I have treasures like that, and I can show them to you. But there may come a time, my friend, when we'll want peace and something richer to feast on.

FAUST. If I ever stretch out on a bed of idleness and go quiet, let that be the end of me at once! If you can flatter me with lies until I'm pleased with myself, if you can seduce me with pleasure until I'm satisfied—then let that day be my last! That's the bet I'm offering. MEPHISTOPHELES. Done! FAUST. And I mean it! The moment I say to the passing instant, 'Stay a while! You are so beautiful'—then you can put me in chains, then I'll gladly go to my ruin! Then let the funeral bell toll, then you're free of your service to me, the clock may stop, its hands may break, and let time be over for me.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Think this over carefully—my memory doesn't fail.
FAUST. You're fully entitled to that. I haven't estimated my strength rashly. I'm a slave, whatever I do—whether to you, or to something else, hardly matters.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then today, at the Doctors' banquet, I'll wait on you as your servant. But one more thing—so there's no risk to me, give me a line or two in writing, if you would.

FAUST. So you want a signed document too, you pedant? Have you never known a man, never tested his word? Isn't it enough that what I say today will hold for all my days to come? The world sweeps everything along in its currents—should a mere promise be able to hold my life in place? And yet we carry this illusion in our hearts anyway; who could free himself of it? Blessed is the man whose heart truth keeps pure—he'll never regret any sacrifice he's made. Still, a parchment, written and sealed with care, is a kind of ghost that everyone tries to dodge. The word dies right there in the pen, and the wax and leather end up ruling instead. What do you want from me, base spirit—brass, marble, parchment, paper? Should the terms be carved with a stylus, a pen, or a chisel? I'll leave the choice entirely up to you.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Why work yourself up with such an overblown speech? Any scrap of paper will do for a pact like this—and you'll sign your name with a drop of blood.
FAUST. If that satisfies you fully, then let's go along with the farce.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Blood is a very special kind of fluid.

FAUST. Don't worry that I'll try to break this pact. What I'm promising you is simply the sum total of what I'm striving for anyway. I've puffed myself up far too high; my proper place is right down there with you. The great Spirit gave me no answer, and Nature has shut her gate on me. The thread of thought has finally snapped, and knowledge only leaves me sick with disgust. Let's plunge into the depths of the senses instead, to cool the heat of burning passion! Let every wonder take shape and form behind the impenetrable veil it wears! Let's dive into the wild rush of time, into the churn and roll of circumstance! Let pleasure and pain, success and frustration, follow one another as they will—restless activity is what proves a man!

MEPHISTOPHELES. No bound is set for you, no limit. Whether you want to sample everything, or snatch quick pleasures on the fly, may whatever you get agree with you! Just get started, and don't hold back timidly.

FAUST. But you heard me—this isn't about joy. I'll take the dizzying whirl of it, pleasure's sharpest pain, love mixed with hate, disdain that exhilarates. My mind, having had its fill of longing for knowledge, won't shy away from any suffering from now on, and everything that life has in store for all of humanity, I'll test within my own innermost self: I'll take on the highest and the lowest forms my soul can hold, pile their joy and their misery onto myself, and so expand my single self out to embrace everyone else's—and in the end, like all of them, I'll be wrecked too.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Believe me—I've chewed on this same tough meat for thousands of years now, and no one, from the cradle to the grave, has ever managed to digest this old leaven! Trust one of us on this: this whole cosmic order exists only for a god's enjoyment. He lives in splendor, singular and eternal, but he shoves us off into the dark, out of sight, and hands you nothing but day and night.
FAUST. And yet I will!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now that's the spirit! There's just one thing still worth repeating: art is long, and time is short. So let yourself be taught, I say! Go team up with a poet, let him give free rein to his imagination, and then wear, as your own, the crown made of all the fine qualities of his invention—the courage of a lion, the swiftness of a wild stag, the fiery blood of an Italian, the steady endurance of a Northerner! Let him find for you the secret thread that ties the noble and the base together, and teach your young, pleasure-loving pulse to love by rule and hate by measure! I'd honestly like to meet a man like that myself—Sir Microcosm, we could call him.
