FAUST. What am I, then, if I'm denied the crown of all humanity that every part of me longs for?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, in the end, you are what you are. Pile a wig with a million curls on your head, put on shoes a yard tall—you're still exactly what you are, and nothing hides it.

FAUST. I can feel that I've gathered up all the treasure of human thought and knowledge for nothing; and now, if I sit down to rest, no fresh spring of strength rises in my mind. I haven't grown a hair's breadth taller, I'm not one step closer to the infinite—

MEPHISTOPHELES. My good sir, you're seeing the facts exactly the way everyone sees them. We need to arrange things more cleverly now, before life's pleasures turn stale on us. Good heavens, both your hands and feet, your head, your manhood—those are yours, sure. But is what I freshly indulge in any less fully mine because of that? If I keep six horses in my stable, aren't their strength and speed mine to use as well? I go tearing along, a complete man, as if I had twenty-four legs of my own. So take hold! Let thinking rest, and plunge into the world with real appetite! I tell you—a man lost in speculation is like some beast a demon leads in circles over a barren moor, while all around him lie fresh green pastures.
FAUST. So how do we begin?

MEPHISTOPHELES. We get out of here, into a wider world. What kind of martyrdom is this place! What sense is there, what wisdom, in boring yourself and boring your students to death? Leave that to Neighbor Paunch! Why wear yourself out threshing empty straw forever? The best of what you learn, you don't dare tell the young people anyway—never! I hear footsteps coming this way. FAUST. I haven't got the heart to see him right now.

MEPHISTOPHELES. The poor boy's been waiting so long for an audience, he shouldn't leave uncomforted. Lend me your cap and gown right away! I'll play the part with style. Trust my wits to see me through. I only need about fifteen minutes; meanwhile, get yourself ready for our fine trip.
[He disguises himself.]
[Exit Faust.]
[In Faust's long robe.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. Despise reason and knowledge—the highest powers a man can have! Just let the spirit of lies bind you tight with dazzling magic tricks and I'll have you body and soul, sure and certain! Fate gave this man a bold, unbridled spirit that has to keep pressing forward, ever onward, whose too-hasty drive carries him right past the earthly joys he could have kept. I'll drag him through the wildest life there is, through flat, stale indifference; I'll wear him down with struggle, with chills, with checks, until, for all his hot and insatiable craving, the dream of a drink will mock his thirsty lips without ever satisfying them. He'll beg for refreshment in vain—had he not already sold himself to the Devil, nothing could save him anyway; he'd still be lost forever.
[A student enters.]
STUDENT. I've only just arrived, and I've come, full of devotion and sincerity, to meet and get to know the famous man everyone speaks of to me with such reverence.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Your politeness flatters me. You're looking at a man like any other. Have you perhaps already started elsewhere?

STUDENT. Please take me on now, I beg you—I come to you full of good courage, some money, and healthy blood. My mother could hardly bear to let me go; but I'd really like to learn something worth knowing.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then you've come to just the right place.

STUDENT. I have to admit, I'd like to leave it again already. These walls, these vaulted rooms—I find them anything but pleasant. It's all so cramped and closed-in and mean; you don't see a single tree, not a bit of green, and once I'm in the lecture halls, I lose all sense of seeing, hearing, and thinking.

MEPHISTOPHELES. That's all just a matter of habit. Think how a child, at first, is reluctant to take its mother's milk, but soon can't be coaxed away from it. It'll be the same for you at the breast of Wisdom—every day you'll find it more of a delight.
STUDENT. I'll cling to her gladly and drink her dry—but please, tell me, what's the right way to get at her?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Before you say anything more, tell me which particular field you want to study.
STUDENT. I want the highest learning there is; I'd gladly take in everything there is in earth and heaven, in nature and in science too.
MEPHISTOPHELES. That's exactly the right path for you—though it does demand strict attention.
STUDENT. I'll throw myself into it body and soul; though, I admit, I do have some fondness for a little freedom and recreation on summer holidays.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Use your time well! It slips away from us so fast; but discipline can help you win it back, I promise you. So, friend, to sum up my advice briefly: first, take the collegium logicum. There your mind will be drilled and strapped in tight, as if laced into a pair of Spanish boots, so that it's forced into a heavier, more measured gait along the path of thought, instead of darting here and there like a will-o'-the-wisp in the murky dark. You'll spend whole days learning to be told what you once did in a single stroke, like eating and drinking, easily and naturally—that 'one, two, three!' belongs to it. Really, the fabric of the mind's thinking is a lot like a weaver's masterpiece: one treadle sends a thousand threads flying, shuttles fly back and forth, the threads get knitted together invisibly, and an endless combination results. Then the philosopher steps in and proves it couldn't possibly have been otherwise: the first was thus, the second thus, and therefore the third and fourth are thus; and if the first and second hadn't been, the third and fourth never would have existed either. Students everywhere believe this, but they never manage to become weavers themselves. Anyone who wants to study a living thing first drives the soul out of it by force; then he holds the pieces in his hand, all sorted and classified—except the spiritual bond that held it together is gone. Chemistry calls this 'encheiresis naturae,' and doesn't even realize it's mocking itself with the name!
STUDENT. I can't quite follow you there.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You'll soon get the hang of it, once you've learned to reduce everything to categories you can use.
STUDENT. After all that, I feel as dazed as if a millwheel were spinning inside my head!

MEPHISTOPHELES. And after that—your first and foremost duty—learn the use and beauty of metaphysics! Make sure you profoundly grasp whatever doesn't fit into a human brain at all! There's a splendid word ready to serve, for whatever does or doesn't fit into your mind. But first, for at least this first half year, stick rigidly to a schedule: five hours a day, and be right there when the clock strikes! Prepare ahead of time, with your paragraphs memorized by heart, so you can keep a closer eye and make sure nothing's said that isn't already in the book—and take your notes as tirelessly as if the Holy Spirit himself were dictating to you!
STUDENT. You don't need to tell me twice! I already see how useful it is to write things down: whatever you have in black and white, you can carry home and go over again.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Now, choose yourself a field of study!
STUDENT. I can't bring myself to warm up to Law.

MEPHISTOPHELES. I can't really blame you students for that—I know what that science has become. Every right and law gets passed down like some endless hereditary disease, dragged from one generation to the next, shifted from place to place. Reason turns into nonsense, kindness into a burden. Woe to you for being born a grandchild! As for the right that was born with us, truly ours—no one's in any hurry to think about that.
STUDENT. Your speech only deepens my own disgust. Lucky the man you'll get to teach! I've nearly settled on Theology.

MEPHISTOPHELES. I wouldn't want to see you led astray there either. As for that science, let me warn you—it's very hard to avoid the wrong path in it; there's so much hidden poison lurking inside it, and it looks so much like the medicine that you can hardly tell the difference. Best to listen to just one voice, and simply take your master's words as truth. Fix your attention on the words! Then you'll pass through the safest gate into the halls of certainty.
STUDENT. But surely there has to be some idea behind the word.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Of course! But don't strain yourself trying too hard for that—right where understanding fails, a word steps in promptly to take its place. Words are wonderful for arguing with; you can build whole systems out of words; words are wonderful to believe in; and no one can ever steal so much as a syllable from a word.

STUDENT. Forgive me, I'm keeping you with all these questions. But I have to trouble you once more. Could you say a strong word or two about Medicine? Three years is such a short time, and God knows the field is enormous. If someone could just point me toward some kind of guide, it would be so much easier to feel my way forward.

MEPHISTOPHELES (aside). I'm sick and tired of this dry tone—time to play the Devil properly again. The spirit of Medicine is easy to grasp: study the great world and the small one to your heart's content, and in the end let it all go, just as God wills! It's useless to go drifting through the realms of science—each person only ever learns what he's able to learn; but the one who seizes the moment's gift, he's the right man for it. You're well built, that much is clear—the rest a bold manner will win for you. If you trust yourself, everyone else will trust you too. Learn especially how to handle women! Their endless aches and complaints, in a thousand different keys, all come from one source and are all cured the same way; and if you're even halfway discreet in how you act, you'll always have them at your feet. First, a title has to draw them in and impress them, and show that your art beats all the others; then, by way of greeting, you're free to touch and examine them, something other men spend years pleading for the chance to do. You press and count the beats of her pulse, and then, with a burning sideways glance, you slip your arm around her swelling waist to check whether her corset's laced too tight.
[Aloud.]
STUDENT. Now that's better! At least one can see the how and the where.
MEPHISTOPHELES. My good friend, all theory is gray, and only life's golden tree is green.
STUDENT. I swear, it all feels like a dream to me. Might I be so bold as to ask, once more, to hear your wisdom laid out in full?
MEPHISTOPHELES. As much as I'm able, gladly.
STUDENT. I really can't leave just yet—let me first give you my album to sign; grant me that favor, I beg you!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Of course.
[He writes, and returns the book.]
STUDENT (reads). 'Eritis sicut Deus, scientes bonum et malum.' (You shall be like God, knowing good and evil.) (Closes the book reverently and leaves.)
MEPHISTOPHELES. Just follow that old saying, and my cousin the serpent that you were told to crush underfoot: for all your resemblance to God, you'll still end up a sorry specimen!
[Faust enters.]
FAUST. So, where shall we go now?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Wherever you like. We'll see the small world, then the great one. Think of the pleasure, the profit you'll gain, sailing through the whole course free of charge!

FAUST. But with this long beard I'm wearing, I'll never manage any ease or grace out there. The attempt would be pointless—I never learned how to move through the world. I feel so small next to other people, I'd always be tripping over my own embarrassment.
MEPHISTOPHELES. My friend, you'll soon shake off all such doubts. Just be sure of yourself, and you'll already have the knack of living!
FAUST. But how do we even leave the house? Where's your carriage, your horses, your servants?

MEPHISTOPHELES. We'll simply spread this cloak out properly, and it will carry us through the air. Just make sure, on a flight this bold, that you travel light. I'll conjure up a bit of fire and air, and it will lift us easily above the earth—and if we're not weighed down, we'll travel fast and clear. Congratulations on your new career!

chapters.title: Auerbach's Cellar in Leipzig
paragraphs: [Auerbach's Cellar in Leipzig. Carousal of Jolly Companions.]
FROSCH. Nobody laughing? Nobody drinking? I'll teach you how to grin, just watch. Today you're all like wet straw, so tame—usually you're blazing.
BRANDER. That's on you—we get nothing from you, no filth, no foolishness.
FROSCH. (Pours a glass of wine over Brander's head.) There, both at once!
BRANDER. Twice the pig you are!
FROSCH. You asked for it—I gave you mine.
SIEBEL. Throw out anyone who starts a fight—out the door! Sing full-throated, drink, and roar! Up! Hey! Ho!
ALTMAYER. Lord help me, what a bellow! Somebody bring cotton, quick—that fellow's burst my eardrums.
SIEBEL. When the vault rings with the song, that's when you really notice how deep and strong the bass is.
FROSCH. Well said! And out with anyone who takes offense at the smallest thing! Ah, tara, lara, da!
ALTMAYER. Ah, tara, lara, da!
FROSCH. Throats are warmed up, let's begin! (Sings.) The dear old Holy Roman Empire—how does it even hold together?

BRANDER. What a rotten song! Ugh—a political song, a downright offensive song! Thank God every morning that you don't have the Holy Roman Empire to worry about! At least I count it a real blessing that I'm neither Chancellor nor Kaiser. Still, we do need some kind of head to rule us, so let's elect ourselves a Pope. You all know what quality decides the vote and lifts a man to the top.
FROSCH (sings). Soar up, soar up, nightingale! Carry ten thousand greetings to my sweetheart!
SIEBEL. No greetings to my sweetheart! I'm warning you, I won't stand for it.
FROSCH. Greet my sweetheart and kiss her too! Just try and stop me! Draw the latch, in the dark. Draw the latch, the lover's awake. Shut the latch, morning's breaking.
[Sings.]

SIEBEL. Sure, sing on, keep singing, praise her, brag all you like! I'll save my laugh for the right moment—she led me around by the nose, and now she'll do the same to you. Her lover ought to be some ugly goblin, meeting her for a bit of fun out where four roads cross; some old billy-goat trotting home from the Blocksberg ought to bleat her a randy good-night! A real flesh-and-blood man is far too good for that girl. Greet her? Not me—unless smashing her windows counts as a greeting!

BRANDER (pounding on the table). Attention! Listen to me! Admit it, gentlemen, I know how to live. We've got lovesick men here tonight, and being the kind of host I am, I owe them something fresh, suited to their condition. Pay attention—this one's the latest thing, and everybody join in on the chorus! There was a rat down in the cellar, fattened soft on butter and grease; he had a belly under his coat just like Doctor Luther's. The cook laid out poison for him, craftily, and after that he felt as cramped and wretched as if he had love stuck in his chest.
[He sings.]
CHORUS (shouting). As if he had love stuck in his chest!

BRANDER. He ran around, he scurried about, lapping his thirst from every puddle; he gnawed and scratched the whole house up, but nothing eased his fit. He spun in circles, leapt in torment, driven half mad with pain, and soon enough the poor beast had had it—just as if he had love stuck in his chest.
CHORUS. As if he had love stuck in his chest!

BRANDER. And at last, driven wild in broad daylight, he ran straight into the kitchen, dropped by the hearth, and lay there twitching in his final spasms. And the murderess laughed with glee: 'Ha, ha—he's breathing his last,' she said, 'just as if he had love stuck in his chest!'
CHORUS. As if he had love stuck in his chest!
SIEBEL. Look how the dull fools enjoy that! To me, scattering poison for rats like that is a proper art.
BRANDER. Taking their side warmly now, are you?
ALTMAYER. I've noticed the bald, potbellied one—misfortune's taming him bit by bit; he sees his own natural shape in that poisoned, bloated rat.
[Faust and Mephistopheles.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. Before anything else, I'm bringing you here, where good fellows gather together, so you can see how easily life slips by. For these people every day's a holiday. With not much wit and not much effort, they spin round and round in tight little circles, like kittens chasing their own tails. And as long as no headache plagues them and the landlord keeps extending credit, they live happily, without a care in the world.
BRANDER. It's easy to work out—they've got that odd look of people just back from traveling. They haven't been here an hour.
FROSCH. You've hit it exactly! Leipzig, now, that's a town after my own heart—a miniature Paris, the way it polishes its people.
SIEBEL. Who do you suppose these strangers are?

FROSCH. Leave it to me! I'll get them drinking first, and then, easy as pulling a baby tooth, I'll worm their secret out of them, see if I don't. They're from some noble house, that's plain enough—haughty and dissatisfied, the both of them.
BRANDER. Traveling con men, more like, out on a spree.
ALTMAYER. Could be.
FROSCH. Watch this, I'll smoke them out now!
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). Not even if he had them by the throat would these people ever smell the Devil on us! FAUST. Good greetings, gentlemen!
SIEBEL. Our thanks—same to you. (Muttering, eyeing Mephistopheles from the side.) Is that fellow lame in one foot?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Might we join you for a while? In place of the decent drink one can't seem to find here, your company alone will do just as well.
ALTMAYER. You strike me as a rather particular sort of person.
FROSCH. No doubt you left Rippach late—did you stop and have supper there with Hans, and that's what held you up?
MEPHISTOPHELES. We passed through today without stopping to see him. Last time we spoke, though, he had a lot to say about his cousins, and asked us to pass along his warm greetings to each of them.
[He bows to Frosch.]
ALTMAYER (aside). There, you see—he knows his business.
SIEBEL. A sharp customer, this one.
FROSCH. Just wait, I'll catch him yet.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Unless I'm mistaken, we heard some well-trained voices singing in chorus just now; and truly, a song must ring out beautifully off these vaulted arches.
FROSCH. Are you some kind of virtuoso, by chance?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh no—plenty of enthusiasm, only middling ability.
ALTMAYER. Give us a song, then!
MEPHISTOPHELES. As many as you like.
SIEBEL. Just make sure it's brand new!
MEPHISTOPHELES. We've just come back from Spain, that lovely land of wine and song and sleep. There once was a king who reigned, and he had a great big black flea—
[Sings.]
FROSCH. Listen to that—a flea! Do you get the joke? I call a flea a proper guest.

MEPHISTOPHELES (sings). There once was a king who reigned, and he had a great big black flea, and he loved that flea past all reason, as if it were his own son. He sent for his tailor; the tailor came at once: here, measure the lad for a pair of breeches, and measure him a coat too, I say!
BRANDER. And mind, don't let the tailor take any liberties—warn him, on pain of his life, to measure, cut, and sew with total precision, so the breeches don't have a single wrinkle!

MEPHISTOPHELES. In silk and velvet, gleaming, he was now dressed from head to toe—a coat covered in streaming ribbons, a cross pinned to his chest. He was given the highest rank at once, a minister's star and title, and all his relations too became great lords at court. And the lords and ladies of the court were tormented, awake and in bed; the queen got them on her as well, and her maids were bitten and left bleeding. And none of them dared brush them off or scratch, day or night: but we—we crush them and squash them, the instant one bites!
CHORUS (shouting). We crush them and squash them, the instant one bites! FROSCH. Bravo, bravo, that was splendid!
SIEBEL. May every flea meet the same end!
BRANDER. Point your fingers and pinch them all dead!
ALTMAYER. Hurrah for freedom! Hurrah for wine!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'd gladly drink a glass with you, to freedom's health, if only the wine you've got here were a bit better.
SIEBEL. Let's not hear that remark again!
MEPHISTOPHELES. If I weren't afraid the landlord might complain, I'd gladly treat you fine gentlemen to something from our own cellar's stock.
SIEBEL. Go ahead and treat us—let the landlord take it up with me!
FROSCH. And if the wine's good, you'll get all the praise you like. But don't pour us some stingy little sample—if I'm going to judge its quality, I need a proper mouthful.
ALTMAYER (aside). They're from the Rhine, I'd guess—I thought as much already.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Somebody bring me a gimlet!
BRANDER. What do you need that for? You don't have the casks waiting right outside, do you?
ALTMAYER. There's one right over there, in the landlord's toolbox!
[To Frosch.]
MEPHISTOPHELES (takes the gimlet). Now then, tell me what you'd like.
FROSCH. What do you mean? Do you have that many kinds?
MEPHISTOPHELES. It's entirely up to you—just make your choice.
ALTMAYER (to Frosch). Ha, look at you, licking your lips already, just thinking about it!
FROSCH. Fine—if I get to choose, let it be Rhine wine! Our own fatherland brews the best sparkling wine there is.
[He bores a hole in the edge of the table, at the spot where Frosch is sitting.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Somebody get me a bit of wax, quick, to make stoppers!
ALTMAYER. Ha! I see—it's some kind of conjuring trick.
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Brander). And you?
BRANDER. Champagne for me—let it sparkle, good and fresh!
[He bores again; meanwhile someone has shaped the wax stoppers and plugged the holes with them.]
BRANDER. There's no getting entirely clear of foreign things—good things often aren't close at hand. A true German can't stand the sight or sound of the French, but drinks their wine happily enough.
SIEBEL. (as Mephistopheles approaches his seat) For my part, sour wine's no good to me—fill my glass with something sweet, would you?
MEPHISTOPHELES (boring). Tokay will flow for you right away!
ALTMAYER. No—look me straight in the eye, gentlemen! I can see you're having a laugh at our expense.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh no—with gentlemen of your standing, that would be going too far. Speak up, quickly, make your choice! What vintage can I pour you?
ALTMAYER. Any kind at all—just satisfy us.
[After the holes have been bored and plugged.]

MEPHISTOPHELES (with strange gestures). Grapes grow on the vine, horns grow on the billy-goat! Grapes are juicy, vines are wood—the wooden table can give wine just as good! Look deep into Nature's workings—only believe, and here's a miracle for you! Now pull the stoppers, and drink your fill!
[As they pull out the stoppers, and the wine each man wished for flows into his glass.]
ALL. Oh, beautiful fountain, flowing as we please!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Just be careful you don't spill any!
[They drink repeatedly.]
ALL (sing). We feel like five hundred hogs, wonderfully, beastly jolly!
MEPHISTOPHELES. See how happy the poor creatures are now—free as anything!
FAUST. I'd rather we left them to it.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Wait, just watch first—their animal side is about to put on a splendid show.
[He drinks carelessly; the spilled wine turns to flame on the ground.]
SIEBEL. Help! Fire! Help! It's hellfire!
MEPHISTOPHELES (charming away the flame). Quiet down, friendly element! That was just a small taste of purgatory, this time.
[To the revelers.]
SIEBEL. What do you think you're doing? Wait—you'll pay dearly for that! It seems you don't know who you're dealing with.
FROSCH. Don't try that trick on us a second time!
ALTMAYER. I think we'd better send him packing, quietly.
SIEBEL. What, sir! You dare take such liberties, playing your hocus-pocus on us?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Quiet, you old wine barrel.
SIEBEL. Broomstick, is it! You'd insult us to our faces, you impudent thing?
BRANDER. Just wait—a shower of blows is coming your way.
ALTMAYER. (pulls a stopper out of the table; fire shoots into his face.) I'm burning! I'm burning!
SIEBEL. It's sorcery! Strike him down—the man's an outlaw! Cut him to pieces! (They draw their knives and rush at Mephistopheles.)
MEPHISTOPHELES (with solemn gestures). False word, false shape of air—change places now, and fool the senses! Be here—and there!
[They stand there dumbfounded, staring at one another.]
ALTMAYER. Where am I? What a beautiful country!
FROSCH. Vineyards? Can I believe my eyes?
SIEBEL. And purple grapes, right here!
BRANDER. Look, over this green arbor—what a vine, what grapes hanging down!
[He takes Siebel by the nose; the others do the same to one another, and raise their knives.]
MEPHISTOPHELES (as before). Loosen the blindfold of error from their eyes, and let them see now how the Devil likes his joke!
[He vanishes with Faust; the revelers jump apart, startled.]
SIEBEL. What just happened?
ALTMAYER. How do you mean?
FROSCH. Was that your nose I had hold of?
BRANDER (to Siebel). And is that yours I've still got in my hand?
ALTMAYER. That went through me like a jolt, head to foot! Get me a chair, I'm sinking—my head's spinning.
FROSCH. No, but tell me, what actually happened?
SIEBEL. Where is he? If I get my hands on that scoundrel, he won't leave here alive, I swear it.

ALTMAYER. I saw him with my own eyes, riding out through the cellar door on a wine cask, just now. My feet still feel like lead with the fright. (Turning toward the table.) I wonder—could the wine still be flowing?
SIEBEL. It was all a trick, a lie, a sham!
FROSCH. And yet it certainly felt like I was drinking real wine.
BRANDER. But what about the grapes—how do you explain that?
ALTMAYER. Well, tell me now, who's still going to say there's no such thing as miracles!

chapters.title: Witch's Kitchen
paragraphs: [On a low hearth stands a big cauldron over a fire. Strange shapes rise and drift in the steam from the pot. A female ape sits beside it, skimming the surface and watching so it doesn't boil over. The male ape sits nearby with the little ones, warming himself. The ceiling and walls are hung with every kind of bizarre witch's paraphernalia.]
[Faust. Mephistopheles.]

FAUST. These lunatic trappings of witchcraft disgust me! Are you telling me I'll get well again through this insane, chaotic charade? Am I supposed to beg help from some old hag? And is her filthy brew really going to strip thirty years off my life? God help me, can't you come up with anything better! There's another hope dashed. Hasn't nature, hasn't some noble mind, ever discovered a real cure?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Now you're talking sense again, my friend. There is a simpler, more natural way to make you young — but it's written in a different book, and it's a very strange chapter.
FAUST. Still, I want to hear it.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Fine — here's the method, and it needs no gold, no magic, no doctor. Go out to some field, take up a hoe, and dig; keep your life and your mind confined to a narrow little world; eat nothing but plain food; live like an ox among oxen, and don't think it's theft to manure the very field you harvest from — trust me, that's the best way there is to stay young for eighty years!
FAUST. I'm not used to that — I can't stoop to it, taking a spade in hand and working it. That cramped kind of existence isn't for me at all.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then it has to be the witch who helps you.
FAUST. Why does it have to be the hag, and only her? Can't you brew the potion yourself?

MEPHISTOPHELES. That would be a fine way to spend my time, I admit — I'd rather build a thousand bridges meanwhile. It isn't only art and science that do the job; patience has to go into the work too. A calm mind labors a long time at this kind of creation; only time can bring the delicate fermentation to strength. And everything that belongs to it is strange and rare, however you look at it: the devil taught the recipe, true enough — but even the devil can't just make it happen. (Noticing the animals) Look at this delicate pair! That one's the female, this one's the male! (To the animals) It seems your mistress has stepped out?
THE ANIMALS. Off carousing today! Out and away, right up the chimney!
MEPHISTOPHELES. How long does she usually take over her revels?
THE ANIMALS. About as long as it takes us to warm our paws.
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). What do you make of these tender little creatures?
FAUST. More absurd than anything I've ever seen.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Actually, this is exactly the kind of conversation I find most charming! But tell me, you damned puppets, why are you stirring that porridge?
[To the animals.]
THE ANIMALS. We're cooking watery soup for beggars.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then you'll have a large clientele.
[The male ape comes up and fawns on Mephistopheles.]
THE MALE APE. Oh, throw the dice! Make me rich in a trice, let me win for once! Everything's badly run, and if only I had gold, I'd have my wits about me too.
MEPHISTOPHELES. How happy this ape would be if he could try his luck at the lottery!
[Meanwhile the young apes have been playing with a large ball, which they now roll forward.]

THE MALE APE. The world's the ball: it rises and falls, and keeps on rolling; it rings like glass — a hollow thing. How soon will it crack and drop, gone still? Here it gleams bright, here brighter still: I'm alive, right now! Dear son, I tell you, stay away! Your fate is already spoken! It's made of clay, and it will break.
MEPHISTOPHELES. What's the sieve for?
THE MALE APE (taking it down). If you were the thief, I'd know you and shame you. [To Mephistopheles] Look through the sieve! Do you know the thief, and dare not name him?
[He runs to the female ape and lets her look through it.]
MEPHISTOPHELES (approaching the fire). And what's this pot?
MALE APE AND FEMALE APE. The fool doesn't know! He doesn't know the pot, he doesn't know the kettle!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Insolent beast!
THE MALE APE. Here, take the brush at least, and sit yourself down on the bench!
[He invites Mephistopheles to sit down.]
[Faust, who all this while has been standing before a mirror, now approaching it, now stepping back.]

FAUST. What am I seeing? What heavenly form shows itself through the glass, from some fair magic realm! Oh, love, lend me your swiftest wings and carry me into her lovely domain! Ah, if I try to leave this spot, if I dare venture nearer, her beauty grows dim, as if seen through drifting mist! — A woman's shape, glowing with loveliness! Can a woman really be this beautiful? Must I really believe that reclining body is the shining sum of everything heaven holds? Can the earth possibly hold anything to match it?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, naturally — if a god works himself hard for six days and then, quite pleased with himself, says 'excellent,' the result is bound to be something fine. This time, feast your eyes to your heart's content! I'll still track down your sweetheart and snare her for you, and lucky is the man who someday gets to carry her home as his bride. (Sitting like a king on a throne) So here I sit, holding the scepter — all I lack is the crown.
[Faust keeps gazing into the mirror. Mephistopheles, stretching out on the bench and playing with the brush, goes on talking.]
[The animals, who till now have been performing all sorts of strange antics together, bring a crown to Mephistopheles with a great racket.]
THE ANIMALS. Oh, be so kind as to glue the crown together, with sweat and with blood! There, it's done, let it be! We talk and we see, we hear and we rhyme!
[They handle the crown clumsily and break it into two pieces, then leap around with them.]
FAUST (before the mirror). Oh no! I feel I'm losing my mind.
MEPHISTOPHELES (pointing at the animals). My own head is really about to spin, too.
THE ANIMALS. If our luck holds and everything fits — those are thoughts, and we're thinking them!
FAUST (as before). My chest is burning with that sweet vision; let's get away from here at once!
MEPHISTOPHELES (in the same posture). One thing you have to admit — these creatures are genuine, sincere poets.

[The cauldron, which the female ape has neglected to watch all this time, begins to boil over: a great flame shoots up and blazes out of the chimney. The Witch comes plunging down through the flame with terrible shrieks.]

THE WITCH. Ow! ow! ow! ow! You damned beast, you cursed sow! Leaving the kettle to go and singe your mistress! Cursed creature! What's this here? Who are you? What do you want? Who's crept in on us? Let the fire-pain scorch your bones and brain!
[Noticing Faust and Mephistopheles.]
[She plunges the ladle into the cauldron and flings flames toward Faust, Mephistopheles, and the animals. The animals whimper.]
[Reversing the brush he's been holding, and striding among the jars and glasses.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. In two! In two! There goes the brew! There goes the glass! It's just a joke, you foul old ass, keeping time to your crew's singing. Ha! Do you know me? Abomination that you are! Don't you recognize your lord and master, at last? What's stopping me from striking you and your monkey-imps down right now with a proper disaster? Have you no respect for the scarlet coat? Don't you recognize the tall cock's feather anymore? Have I hidden this face of mine? Must I actually tell you my name, you old piece of leather?
[As the Witch shrinks back, full of rage and horror.]
THE WITCH. Oh, forgive me, sir, for the rough greeting! But I don't see the cloven hoof — and where are your two ravens now?

MEPHISTOPHELES. This time I'll let you off the hook — after all, it really has been quite a while since the two of us last met. Civilization, which polishes up the whole world, has rubbed off on the devil too. That old northern phantom is a thing of the past: where do you see horns, tail, and claws on me anymore? And as for the foot, which I really can't do without — it would only make people avoid me — so, like many a spindly young dandy, I've worn false calves for years now.
THE WITCH (dancing). I'm losing my mind and my senses, seeing young master Satan here again!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Woman, keep off that name!
THE WITCH. Why so? What has it ever done to you?

MEPHISTOPHELES. It's been written into the storybooks for ages now — and yet men are none the better for it. The Evil One is gone, but the evil ones remain. Call me Baron, and that'll do fine; I'm a gentleman like any other in my manners. You've no doubt about my noble blood — look, here's the coat of arms I'm wearing!
[He makes an indecent gesture.]
THE WITCH (laughing uncontrollably). Ha! Ha! That's just like you, I know it well — you were always a rogue, and you still are.
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). My friend, pay close attention, please! This is exactly how you handle a witch.
THE WITCH. Gentlemen, how can I be of service?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Give us a goblet of that famous juice of yours! But I must ask for the very oldest brew — age doubles its strength.

THE WITCH. Gladly! Here's a bottle I sometimes sip from myself, and it doesn't stink in the least; I'll happily pour him a glass. Only — if this man drinks it without the proper preparation, as you well know, it'll kill him within the hour.
[Whispering.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. He's a friend of mine, it'll suit him fine, and he deserves the best your kitchen can offer. Come, draw your circle, speak your incantation, and fill the goblet to the brim!

[The Witch, with fantastic gestures, draws a circle and arranges strange objects inside it; meanwhile the glasses begin to ring and the cauldron to hum, making a kind of music. Finally she brings out a great book, stations the apes inside the circle to serve as a reading-stand and to hold the torches, then beckons Faust to come closer.]
FAUST (to Mephistopheles). Now, what's supposed to come of this? These crazy creatures, this insane stuff, these frantic gestures — all this repulsive trickery — I know it, and I despise it.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, nonsense! It's all a bit of a joke — don't be so terribly severe about it! She has to play doctor and put on her act, so that afterward the drink can do its proper work.
[He talks Faust into stepping into the circle.]
[Begins declaiming from the book with great emphasis.]

THE WITCH. See, this is how it's done! Make ten from one, and let two go, then make three even, and you'll be rich. Drop the four! From five and six — that's the witch's trick — make seven and eight, and there you have it! And nine is one, and ten is none. That's the witch's own arithmetic!
FAUST. She talks like someone raving in a fever.

MEPHISTOPHELES. You'll hear a lot more before we're done with her. I know it well — I could recite the whole book; I've wasted enough time on that kind of history. A perfect contradiction like that is always a mystery to the wise and the foolish alike. The art is both ancient and new — every age has been taught the same trick, scattering error instead of truth by way of three and one, and one and three. People chatter and lecture, and nobody objects; everyone shrinks from keeping company with fools. Usually a person believes that, if he only hears words, there must be some real thought behind them too!
THE WITCH (continuing). The highest wisdom of learning stays hidden deep from everyone — to the one who doesn't bother thinking, it's handed over, freely, unasked for!
FAUST. What nonsense she's spouting at us! My head feels ready to split, I swear — it's like listening to a hundred thousand fools all talking at once.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh excellent prophetess, enough of the incantation! Just bring us your drink now, and fill the cup quickly to the brim! This draft won't hurt my friend in the least — he's a man of many accomplishments and has downed plenty of drinks in his time.
[The Witch, with much ceremony, pours the drink into a cup; as Faust raises it to his lips, a small flame flares up.]
[The Witch breaks the circle; Faust steps out of it.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. And now, away! You mustn't linger.
THE WITCH. And may the drink do you a world of good!
MEPHISTOPHELES (to the Witch). Save your wish for Walpurgis Night — whatever favor I owe you, I'll grant it then.
THE WITCH. Here's a song — if you sing it now and then, you'll find it has a peculiar effect.

MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). Come, let's walk at once! Some brisk exercise has to bring on the sweat you need, and send the drink's power coursing through your whole body. Then I'll teach you to prize a noble kind of idleness, and soon enough you'll feel, with the keenest thrill of pleasure, how Cupid stirs and leaps on his light, restless wings.
FAUST. Just let me take one quick look in the mirror again — how beautiful that woman was!
MEPHISTOPHELES. No, no! Believe me, you'll soon see the paragon of all women, alive and warm, in the flesh. Once this drink gets into your blood, you'll find every woman looks like Helen!
[Aside.]

chapters.title: Street
paragraphs: [Faust. Margaret (passing by).]
FAUST. Fair lady, please don't be offended if I offer you my arm and my company!
MARGARET. I'm no lady, and I'm not fair, and I can get myself home without your help.
[She frees herself and exits.]

FAUST. By heaven, that girl is wonderfully lovely! I've never seen anyone to compare with her — so sweetly virtuous and pure, and yet with a bit of an edge to her too! That red lip, that clear glow in her cheek — I won't forget them as long as I live! The way she lowered her shy eyes is stamped deep in my heart; and how curt and sharp she was with me — that was pure delight!
[Mephistopheles enters.]
FAUST. Listen — I want that girl, I have to have her!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Which one?
FAUST. The one who just walked by.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Her? She's coming straight from confession, absolved of every sin — I was standing right behind her chair, listening in. She's so innocent, in fact, that she barely had anything to confess. I have no power over souls that pure.
FAUST. And yet she's older than fourteen.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now you're talking like some rake who wants every flower for himself, and imagines there's no favor, no honor, reserved for anyone but him — though it doesn't always work out that way.

FAUST. Most worthy schoolmaster, spare me! Don't lecture me on morals! I'm telling you plainly, I claim my full right to her; and if that vision of delight isn't resting in my arms tonight, then our pact is broken at midnight.
MEPHISTOPHELES. But think about how these things actually work! I need at least a fortnight just to find the right opportunity.
FAUST. If I had even seven hours, I wouldn't need the devil's help at all — I'd win her over myself.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now you're talking like a Frenchman! But please, don't take offense — why rush to burn through all the joy at once? Your pleasure will be far less if you go straight for it than if you work her slowly with all sorts of tender maneuvering, and shape and mold her to your purpose the way it's done in Italian romances.
FAUST. I have appetite enough without all that.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Now, enough joking! I'm telling you once and for all — speed will get you nowhere with this girl. She can't be taken by storm; we'll have to use strategy.
FAUST. Get me something that belongs to the angel! Take me to where she sleeps! Get me a scarf from her breast — a garter that's touched her knee!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Just so you see how eager I am to help ease your suffering, we won't waste another minute — I'll find her room today and take you there.
FAUST. And will I see her — have her?
MEPHISTOPHELES. No! She has to go to a neighbor's. Meanwhile you can sit there alone, glowing with every hope of pleasure to come, breathing in her presence to your heart's content.
FAUST. Can we go there now?
MEPHISTOPHELES. It's still too early.
FAUST. Get me a gift for her! [Exit.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Presents already? Good — that's sure to win her over. I know plenty of pleasant spots and buried treasures from long ago; I'll have to go dig up something. [Exit.

chapters.title: Evening
paragraphs: [A small, neatly kept room.]
[Braiding and pinning up her hair.]

MARGARET. I'd give something to know who that gentleman was today. He certainly looked like a fine man, and from a good family too — and I could tell a lot from his face, or else he wouldn't have been so bold.
[Exit.]
[Mephistopheles. Faust.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Come in, but quietly — follow me!
FAUST (after a moment's silence). Leave me alone here, please!
MEPHISTOPHELES (poking around). Not every girl keeps things this tidy.

FAUST (looking around). Oh, welcome, soft and sweet twilight, that fills this hallowed little shrine! Sweet pain of love, bind with your quick chains this heart that's been starving on the mere dew of hope! What a sense of quiet, order, and contentment surrounds everything here! What abundance lives in this poverty! What happiness is packed into this narrow little room! Take me in, you chair, that once gathered joy and sorrow into your open arms! How often the children, rosy-cheeked, must have hung here around this very seat where their father sat! Perhaps my darling, among the crowd of children, grateful for some Christmas gift, once kissed her grandfather's withered hand right here. I feel, dear girl, your very spirit of order and contentment whispering around me — the spirit that guides you with its motherly hand, that tells you to spread the cloth smooth on your table, that makes the sand beneath your feet lie whiter and crisper. Oh dearest hand, it's you who turns this hut into a heaven on earth! And here! What sweetest thrill runs through my blood! I could spend whole hours here, lingering: here nature shaped, as if at play, the angel out of the mere bud. Here the child lay, her tender chest filled with life's warm essence, and here, through some holier and purer presence, the more divine shape was formed. And me? What power drew me here? How deeply I'm moved, this hour! What am I after? Why is my heart so full, so sore? Wretched Faust! I hardly recognize myself anymore. Is there some kind of magic vapor here? I came craving a moment's pleasure, and instead I'm dissolved in dreams of love's sweet ease! Are we just playthings of every passing mood in the air? And if she walked in on me right now, how I'd have to answer for it! How small this great oaf would suddenly be, stretched limp and tender at her feet!
[He throws himself into a leather armchair by the bed.]
[He lifts one of the bed-curtains.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Quick! I see her coming back.
FAUST. Go! Go! I'm not leaving.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Here's a little box, not a bad one, that I picked up elsewhere just now. Set it in the cupboard, quick! I swear it'll turn her head to see it — I've put some trinkets inside for you, to win another girl with. True, a child's a child, and play is play.
FAUST. I don't know — should I really do it?

MEPHISTOPHELES. You're asking? Maybe you'd rather keep the little trinket yourself! Then let me suggest — spare this fine day your appetite, and spare me the extra trouble. You're not stingy, I trust? I'm rubbing my hands together just thinking about it — now hurry, get moving! Betray the sweet young thing so she bends to your every wish and will; and here you stand looking as if you were being marched off to a lecture hall, with physics and metaphysics both looming gray and dreary in front of you! But go, quickly! [Exeunt.
[He puts the box in the cupboard and locks it again.]

MARGARET (with a lamp). It's so stuffy, so close in here! And yet it's not that warm outside. I feel — I don't know why — such fear! If only mother would come home! Where can she be? I'm shivering, chilled all over — I'm such a silly, timid thing! There once was a king in Thule, faithful until the grave, to whom his dying mistress gave a golden goblet. Nothing was dearer to him; he drained it at every feast; his eyes filled with tears every time he drank from it. When his time came to die, he counted up all the towns in his land, and left them all to his heir, denying him nothing — except the golden goblet. He sat at the royal banquet with his knights of high rank, in the lofty hall of his ancestors, in the castle by the sea. There the old reveler stood and drank down his last spark of life, then hurled the sacred goblet down into the waves below. He watched it plunge, fill, and sink deep into the sea; then his eyelids closed forever, and never again did he drink. — How did this lovely box get here to me? I locked the cupboard, I'm quite sure. It's truly strange! What could be inside it? Maybe someone left it as security for a loan, and mother lent against it? And here's a key that fits it: I have half a mind to open it. What's this? Good God in heaven! Where did such things come from? I've never seen anything so beautiful! Rich jewelry, the kind a noble lady might wear on the grandest holiday! How would this pearl necklace look in my hair? Ah, who could own all this splendor? If only the earrings were mine alone! One looks so different with things like these. What good does youth and beauty do you? You may have them, fine and well, but people don't care about you any the more for it. They praise you, sure, but half out of pity — everything, everything comes down to gold, depends on gold. Poor us!
[She opens the window.]
[She begins to sing while undressing.]
[She opens the cupboard to arrange her clothes and notices the box of jewelry.]
[She puts on the jewelry and stands before the mirror.]

chapters.title: Promenade
paragraphs: [Faust, walking up and down thoughtfully. Mephistopheles comes to him.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. By every love that's ever been spurned! By the hottest, most merciless hellfire! I wish I knew something worse to swear by!
FAUST. What's wrong with you? What's got hold of you, you goblin? I've never seen a face like that on you.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'd hand myself straight over to the devil, if I weren't already one myself!
FAUST. Your head's badly out of order — it really suits you, going around raving mad.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Just imagine — the jewelry left for Margaret has ended up in a priest's pocket! Her mother spotted them and instantly a secret dread came over her. That woman has a keen nose for anything tainted — she goes sniffing through her prayer book and smells out every single object, to see whether it's sacred or profane. And from every gem she could just tell there wasn't much blessing attached to them. 'My child,' she said, 'ill-gotten gains snare the soul and poison the blood. We'll lay this before the Mother of God — she'll pay us back in heavenly manna!' But Margaret thought to herself, with a sour look, 'You don't look a gift horse in the mouth, and surely whoever gave me these things can't be godless.' The mother had a priest sent for; he saw right away what game was afoot, and looked the whole thing over with a sly kind of favor. He said: 'Now that's the right way to look at it — whoever overcomes, also wins. The Holy Church has a healthy stomach — she's swallowed whole countries as forfeit before, and never once complained of being too full. The Church alone, without question, has the right digestion for ill-gotten goods.'
FAUST. That's a common enough practice — kings and Jews do the same.

MEPHISTOPHELES. So he pocketed the bracelets, chains, and rings as if they were nothing but toadstools, thanked them no more and no less than if he'd been handed a sack of nuts, promised them the fullest reward in heaven — and they went away feeling deeply edified.
FAUST. And Margaret?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Sits there restless, not knowing what to do or want; thinks about the jewels day and night, but even more about the man who gave them to her.
FAUST. The darling's unhappiness pains me. Go get her another set! The first one wasn't even that impressive.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh yes, to you, sir, it's all just child's play!
FAUST. Arrange it exactly as I want; and work on her neighbor too! Don't just stand there being a dull, sluggish devil — get her some fresh jewelry, something to her taste!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, gracious sir, absolutely, at your command! An infatuated fool like you would blow the sun, the moon, and every star in the sky just to give his sweetheart a bit of entertainment.
[Exit Faust.]
[Exit.]

chapters.title: The Neighbour's House
paragraphs: MARTHA (alone). God forgive my husband, but he hasn't done right by me! Off he went into the world, and left me lying like straw where I'd fallen. And truly, I never did anything to upset him: God knows I loved him, and I can't forget him! Maybe he's even dead! Oh, the misery! If only I had a certificate to prove it!
[She weeps.]
MARGARET (entering). Dame Martha!
MARTHA. Margaret! What's happened to you?

MARGARET. I can hardly stand, my knees are shaking! I found a box in my cupboard, just like the first one — made of ebony, and full of things even more splendid than before, and far richer than the last ones.
MARTHA. You mustn't tell your mother about it! It would go straight to the priest, just like the last one.
MARGARET. Oh, just look — just look at it!
MARTHA (decking her out). Oh, what a blessed stroke of luck for you!
MARGARET. But oh — I daren't wear them out in the street, or be seen with them at church.

MARTHA. Still, you can slip over here often, and put the jewels on in secret, and walk up and down for an hour in front of that mirror over there — we'll have our own private fun with it. And then some occasion will come along, some holiday, when you can show the things off little by little in public — a chain first, then some other piece. Your mother won't notice, and we'll invent some story.
MARGARET. Who could possibly have brought me such precious things? Something about it doesn't feel right, I'm sure of it. Good heavens! Could it have been my mother?
[A knock.]
MARTHA (peeking through the curtain). It's some strange gentleman. Come in!
[Mephistopheles enters.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Forgive me for barging in so boldly, ladies, I beg your pardon. I'm looking for Martha Schwerdtlein!
[Steps back respectfully upon seeing Margaret.]
MARTHA. That's me: what does the gentleman want?
MEPHISTOPHELES (aside to her). It's enough that you're the one — you have a visitor of high standing. Forgive the liberty I've taken — I'll come back this afternoon.
MARTHA (aloud). Well, of all things! Just listen to this — he takes you for a lady, my dear!
MARGARET. I'm just a poor young girl — the gentleman is far too kind. These jewels don't even belong to me.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, it's not just the jewelry — it's your look, your bearing, that gives it away. I'm delighted that I get to stay!
MARTHA. What is it you want? I'd like to know—
MEPHISTOPHELES. I wish I had happier news to bring! Don't hold it against me for saying it plainly: your husband is dead, and sends his regards.
MARTHA. Dead? Oh, that faithful heart! My husband, dead! Just let me die too!
MARGARET. Oh, dear lady, don't lose heart!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Let me tell you the sad story.
MARGARET. That's exactly why I'd never fall in love, I swear it — a loss like that would be the death of me.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Joy follows sorrow, and sorrow comes flying right after joy.
MARTHA. Tell me how his life ended!
MEPHISTOPHELES. He's buried in Padua, beside the good Saint Anthony, in a properly consecrated grave, made for a cool, eternal rest.
MARTHA. Did he leave you any other message?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, one important one, given with many sighs: three hundred masses, to be bought to save his soul from damnation! Otherwise, my hands are empty.
MARTHA. What! Not even a coin? Not a single trinket? The kind of thing any journeyman keeps tucked in his pack as a keepsake, and would rather starve or beg than part with?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Madam, it grieves me to say it — but I give you my word, his money was put to proper use. Besides, his remorse weighed on him terribly, and he lamented his hard luck all the more for it.
MARGARET. Oh, how unlucky people can be! I'll certainly say many a prayer for his soul.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You deserve a swift marriage proposal — you're so kind, so full of sympathy.
MARGARET. Oh, no! It's much too soon for that.
MEPHISTOPHELES. If not a husband, then a sweetheart for the meantime! It's one of heaven's greatest blessings, to have someone dear to hold close.
MARGARET. That's not the custom in this country.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Custom or not — it happens anyway.
MARTHA. Go on, please!

MEPHISTOPHELES. I stood by his deathbed. It was something a little better than manure — half-rotten straw — and yet he died a Christian, sure enough, though he found he had heavier debts on his account than he'd reckoned. He cried out: 'I find my whole conduct hateful! Leaving my wife, my trade, in such an ungrateful way! Ah, the memory of it is killing me! If only I could be forgiven for the wrong I did her!'
MARTHA (weeping). The dear, good man! He was forgiven long ago.
MEPHISTOPHELES. 'And yet,' he said, 'God knows, she was more to blame than I was.'
MARTHA. He lied! What! Slandering me on the brink of death?

MEPHISTOPHELES. His mind was wandering in his final throes, if I can judge such things even half rightly. He said: 'I never had time to play, to breathe freely — first children, then work to put bread on the table for them, bread in every sense of the word, just grinding on, and I couldn't even eat my own share in peace and quiet!'
MARTHA. Had he forgotten all my love, all my loyalty — my work and worry, day and night?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Not at all — the memory of it moved him deeply. He said: 'When I sailed away from Malta, I prayed fervently for my wife and children, and heaven granted us such luck that we captured a Turkish merchant ship carrying a great treasure meant for the Sultan. Then I got my fair share of it, as was only right, since bravery was paid its full reward.'
MARTHA. How? Where? Did he bury it somewhere?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Who knows now which way the four winds have scattered it? A pretty young woman took him in when he was wandering, friendless, around Naples; and she gave him so much love, so much devotion, that he felt it for the rest of his days.
MARTHA. The villain! Stealing from his own children! Even with all that misery weighing on him, it couldn't stop him from living so shamefully!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, but look — he's dead because of it now, in the end. If I were in your position, I wouldn't hesitate — I'd mourn him properly for a year, and meanwhile keep an eye out for another.

MARTHA. Ah, God, I'll hardly find another one as dear as my first was — the world isn't likely to give me that twice. There never was a sweeter fool than mine, only he loved to wander off and leave me, chasing foreign women and foreign wine, and that damned habit of throwing dice, on top of it all.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, well! That might have worked out fine, after all, if he'd been just as easygoing about your little slips. I swear, on that condition, I'd trade rings with you myself.
MARTHA. Oh, the gentleman is pleased to joke.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'd better cut this short and get out of here — she'd take the devil at his word, I'm afraid. (To Margaret) How's that heart of yours doing?
[To Margaret.]
MARGARET. What does the gentleman mean?
MEPHISTOPHELES (aside). What an innocent little thing you are! (Aloud) Ladies, farewell!
[Aloud.]
MARGARET. Farewell!

MARTHA. Wait, one moment before you go! I'd like to have a proper legal witness — where, how, and when he died, to have it all certified. I've always hated doing things irregularly; I want his death put in the weekly paper.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, my good lady, two witnesses always establish the truth. I have a friend, a man of high standing, who'll add his own testimony too. I'll bring him here.
MARTHA. Please do, good sir!
MEPHISTOPHELES. And this young lady will be here too? A fine young man — he's traveled widely; ladies are always delighted by him.
MARGARET. I'd blush with embarrassment in front of him.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Not in front of any king alive, I promise you.
MARTHA. Behind the house, in my garden then — we'll expect the gentlemen there this evening.

chapters.title: Street (II)
paragraphs: [Faust. Mephistopheles.]
FAUST. Well? Is it moving along? Will it be ready soon?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Ah, bravo! So you're burning, are you? Good—Margaret will soon put out that fire. You'll meet her this evening at neighbor Martha's. There's no woman better suited to play the pimp and the fortune-teller!
FAUST. Good.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Still, something's wanted from us in return.
FAUST. One favor deserves another.
MEPHISTOPHELES. All we have to do is swear a statement that her husband's body—stiff and pale by now—lies buried in holy ground at Padua.
FAUST. Very clever! And I suppose first we'll have to make the trip there?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Sancta simplicitas! No need for that kind of trouble. Swear to it whether you know anything or not!
FAUST. If you've nothing better than that, I'll tear up your fine little scheme.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, now there you go! Such a saint! Is this the first time in your life you've been asked to bear false witness? Haven't you handed out definitions of God, the world, and everything in it, of man and everything that stirs his soul—with a straight face and a bold heart? And if you look at it honestly, didn't you know just as little about all that as you know now about where Schwerdtlein died and was buried—you'll have to admit it!
FAUST. You are, and you'll always be, a liar and a sophist.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes—if I didn't see through you so well. Because tomorrow, in all honor, won't you be flattering poor Margaret, swearing her your whole soul's devotion, playing the perfect lover?
FAUST. And meaning it, from my heart.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Very nice! Eternal loyalty, eternal love, this one all-powerful passion of yours—will that come from the heart too?

FAUST. Stop, stop! It will! When I feel it—when I search for a name for this feeling, this power, and can't find one; when I range through all creation with every sense straining for words, and call this passion, rising to the heavens, endless, eternal, eternal—is that just a devil's trick, a lie?
MEPHISTOPHELES. And still I'm right.

FAUST. Listen—I beg you—spare my breath from here on: whoever wants to be right, and has a clever enough tongue, will always manage it. Come on, I'm sick of talking—you're right, mostly because I have no choice.

chapters.title: Garden
paragraphs: [Margaret on Faust's arm. Martha and Mephistopheles walking back and forth.]

MARGARET. I can tell the gentleman is only humoring me, lowering himself out of kindness, and it embarrasses me. A traveler gets used to making do with whatever company he finds. I know perfectly well that someone like me, with so little to say, can't hold the interest of a man who's seen so much of the world.
FAUST. A single look from you, a single word, means more to me than all the wisdom of the cleverest minds.
[He kisses her hand.]

MARGARET. Please, don't trouble yourself! How could you want to kiss it? It's so rough and ugly! Think of all the work I have to do—it's hard, and there's no end to it. My mother keeps a close eye on me too.
[They walk on.]
MARTHA. And you, sir—always traveling, are you?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Ah, it's the curse of business and duty! There are so many places you have to tear yourself away from, and you're never allowed to simply stay.
MARTHA. In wild young years that kind of life suits a man—roaming the world footloose and free. But then the hard days come, and no one ever speaks well of a bachelor creeping alone into his grave.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I shudder just thinking of that fate closing in.
MARTHA. Then, good sir, you'd better improve your chances while there's time!
[They walk on.]
MARGARET. Yes—out of sight, out of mind. You're gracious enough with your manners, but you must have friends elsewhere, and cleverer ones than me.
FAUST. Believe me, dearest, what people call 'clever' is often nothing but vanity and small-mindedness.
MARGARET. How do you mean?
FAUST. Ah, that simplicity and innocence never know their own worth, their own sacred value! That humility, that lowliness—the highest gifts nature hands out so generously—
MARGARET. Just give me a moment of your time to think about—I'll have all the time in the world to think about you, wherever I am!
FAUST. You must be alone a great deal, I imagine?

MARGARET. Yes—our household is small, but it still has to be looked after, you understand. We have no maid: I do the knitting, the sewing, the sweeping, the cooking—early and late, really everything. And my mother is so exact about how a house should be run! Not that we need to scrimp so much—we could actually afford more comfort than most: my father left us a nice little property, a house, a small garden just outside town. But my days are quieter now. My brother's a soldier, and my little sister died. I had a hard time with that child, I won't pretend otherwise, but I'd gladly take all that trouble again—she was so dear to me.
FAUST. An angel, if she was anything like you.

MARGARET. I raised her myself, and she loved me for it. She was born after my father had already died, and my mother seemed past hope at the time—so weak and wretched. It took her a long while to recover. She couldn't even think of nursing the poor little thing herself, so I fed it all alone, with milk and water—it was as good as mine. Rocked in my lap, sung to sleep, it smiled, and tumbled about, and grew strong.
FAUST. That must have been pure happiness for you.

MARGARET. But plenty of exhausting hours too. I kept the cradle by my bed at night: the moment it stirred, I'd know it, even in my sleep. I'd have to feed it, keep it warm against me, and often climb out of bed just to soothe it, rocking it back and forth, restless as it was. Then at daybreak I'd be at the washtub, and after that the marketing, the kitchen—the same thing, day after day, without end. It doesn't leave your spirits in the best shape, sir, but it does teach you to enjoy your food and your rest.
[They walk on.]
MARTHA. Yes, women have it hard, it's true—a stubborn old bachelor is nearly impossible to convert.
MEPHISTOPHELES. It would only take someone like you to do it—I might give up flirting for something better.
MARTHA. Speak plainly, sir—have you never found anyone? Has your heart never been caught anywhere?
MEPHISTOPHELES. As the saying goes: a warm hearth of one's own and a good wife are worth their weight in gold and jewels.
MARTHA. I mean—have you never felt the slightest bit of desire?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Everywhere I've gone, I've been treated very politely, in fact.
MARTHA. What I mean is—were you never touched in earnest?
MEPHISTOPHELES. A man should never let himself joke with the ladies. MARTHA. Ah, you don't understand me at all!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'm sorry I'm so dense—but I am sure of one thing: that you're very kind.
[They walk on.]
FAUST. And you, angel—did you recognize me the moment I came through the garden gate?
MARGARET. Didn't you see? I looked down at once.
FAUST. And you forgive my boldness—the liberty I took when you were leaving the cathedral?

MARGARET. I was flustered—nothing like that had ever happened to me. No one could ever say a word against my conduct. I thought, has he seen something improper, something too free in the way I act? He seemed to think this girl would be easy enough to deal with. I'll admit, I didn't know myself what it was that spoke up for you, right here in my heart—but I was angry with myself for not being able to stay angry with you.
FAUST. Sweet darling!
MARGARET. Wait a moment!
[She picks a daisy and starts pulling off the petals, one by one.]
FAUST. Is that going to be a bouquet?
MARGARET. No, it's just a game.
FAUST. How's that?
MARGARET. Go away—you'll laugh at me. (She pulls off the petals, murmuring to herself.)
FAUST. What are you murmuring?
MARGARET (half aloud). He loves me—he loves me not.
FAUST. You sweet, angelic soul!
MARGARET (continuing). Loves me not—loves me—loves me not— (Plucking the last petal, she cries out with pure delight:) He loves me!
FAUST. Yes, my child! Let that flower's word be a message from heaven for you! He loves you! Do you understand what that means? He loves you!
[He takes both her hands.]
MARGARET. I'm trembling all over!

FAUST. Don't tremble! Let this look, let this warm grip of our hands say what words can't: to give yourself completely, and to feel the joy of giving yourself completely—that has to last forever! Forever!—because if it ended, it would be despair. No, no—no ending, no ending!
MARTHA (coming forward). Night's falling.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, we should be going.

MARTHA. I'd ask you to stay longer, but this town is full of wagging tongues. It's as if people had nothing better to do—no work, no errands—than to spy on everyone else's business. And you become the talk of the town no matter what you do. Where have our two gone off to?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Flown off down that path there—the reckless little summer birds!
MARTHA. He seems even more taken with her.
MEPHISTOPHELES. And she with him. That's just how the world goes!

chapters.title: A Summer House
paragraphs: [Margaret comes in, hides behind the door, puts a finger to her lips, and peeks through the crack.]
MARGARET. He's coming!
FAUST (entering). Ah, you little tease—I've got you! (He kisses her.)
MARGARET (clasping him, and returning the kiss). Dearest man! I love you with all my heart.
[Mephistopheles knocks.]
FAUST (stamping his foot). Who's there?
MEPHISTOPHELES. A friend!
FAUST. A beast!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Time to say goodbye.
MARTHA (coming). Yes, sir, it's late.
FAUST. May I not wait on you again, then? MARGARET. My mother would object—farewell!
FAUST. Must I really go? Farewell!
MARTHA. Goodbye!
MARGARET. And soon we'll meet again!
[Faust and Mephistopheles leave.]

MARGARET. Dear God! How is it that a man can think and know so much? I stand there ashamed, amazed, and say yes to everything he says—a poor, ignorant girl! I can't imagine what he sees in me. [She exits.]

chapters.title: Forest and Cavern
paragraphs: FAUST (alone). Exalted spirit, you gave me, gave me everything I asked for. It wasn't for nothing that you turned your face to me in fire. You gave me nature as a vast kingdom, with the power to feel it and take joy in it. You don't just let me know it coldly, from a distance—you let me look into its deepest heart as into the heart of a friend. You lead the whole procession of living creatures past me, teaching me to recognize my brothers in the air, in the water, in the silent woods. And when the storm roars and grinds through the forest, when the giant firs come crashing down, dragging neighboring branches and trunks with them in their fall, and the hills fill with hollow thunder—then you lead me to a safe cave, then you show me my own self, and in my own breast the deep, mysterious miracles unfold. And when the full moon rises before me with its soothing light, and silvery ghosts of ages past drift toward me out of every cliff face and damp thicket, softening the harsh edge of thought—I understand now that nothing can ever be perfect for a human being. Along with this rapture, which brings me nearer and nearer to the gods, you gave me the companion I can no longer do without, even though, cold and mocking, he cheapens me in my own eyes, and with a single breath, a single word, turns your gifts to nothing. In my chest he fans an unruly fire for that lovely, beautiful form, tirelessly—so that I rush from longing to satisfaction, and in satisfaction, pine again for longing.
[Mephistopheles enters.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Haven't you had enough of this kind of life by now? How can testing yourself like this go on delighting you? It's fine to try it once, but then you need something new.
FAUST. I wish you had better things to do! You've come back just to spoil a good day.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Fine! I'll leave you be, gladly—you wouldn't dare say that to me seriously. Losing you would be no great loss—a crazy, rude, off-putting companion. One has one's hands full day and night with you; there's no telling from that face of yours whether what one does pleases you or not.
FAUST. There—that's your true voice again! That you bore me, I suppose I owe you thanks for that too!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Poor son of earth, how could you have gotten through your life alone, without me? I've cured you, at least for a while, of your feverish imaginings; if it weren't for me, you'd have walked yourself right off this earth by now. What are you doing crouched here in caves and rocky hollows, like an owl blinking in the dark? Why do you feed yourself, like a toad, on wet moss and dripping stone? A fine way to spend your time! The professor in you is still very much alive.
FAUST. Can you even guess what fresh, living strength I draw from being out here in the wilderness? No—if you could guess it, you'd be devil enough to begrudge me the blessing of it.

MEPHISTOPHELES. A blessing straight from the supernatural springs! Lying out on the mountains in the night dew, embracing heaven and earth in rapture, swelling yourself up to godhood, digging with all your longing down through the marrow of the earth, squeezing the whole six days of creation into your narrow chest, tasting—who knows what—your own ecstatic sense of life poured out over everything in lordly pride, casting off your merely earthly self, and then, with that lofty instinct of yours, working your way at last—you won't even say how—to plucking the final flower!
[With a gesture.]
FAUST. Shame on you!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Ah, that stings, doesn't it! You've every right to cry 'shame' at me just now. One doesn't say in front of chaste ears what chaste hearts can't do without, all the same; and for once I won't begrudge you the pleasure of lying to yourself, in moderation. But you won't keep this up for long. You're already worked up past reason, and if it goes on, you'll soon be engaged to madness and horror, no question. Enough of that! Your love sits alone yonder, weighed down and saddened by everything around her. Her thoughts and longings reach for you constantly—she's head over heels in love. Your passion came flooding over her first, like a stream overflowing from melting snow; you filled her and drowned her in it, and now your own stream is running shallow. It seems to me, instead of lording it about in the forest, the noble gentleman ought to think about rewarding this poor foolish young thing's love. Her days drag on unbearably; she stands at her window watching the clouds drift over the old town wall, far away. 'If only I were a little bird!' she sings, all day and half the night. Sometimes she's lively, mostly she's sad, sometimes cried quite past tears; then she goes quiet again—but always lovesick.
FAUST. Serpent! Serpent!
MEPHISTOPHELES (aside). Ha—have I got you now!
FAUST. Get away from me with your filth, you disgrace! Don't speak that most beautiful creature's name, don't bring the longing for her sweet body back before my half-crazed senses!
MEPHISTOPHELES. What do you want, then? She thinks you've run off. And you have, more or less, haven't you.
FAUST. However far away I am, I'm still near her, and love keeps its watch regardless; it never wavers, no matter the distance. I even envy the body of the Lord the touch of her lips at the altar.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Very good! And I've often envied you that pair of twins that graze among the roses.
FAUST. Get away, you pander!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Rail away, it's entertaining. The God who made boy and girl in the first place understood the noblest purpose of his craft, and made sure they'd have the chance to act on it too. Go on, then! This is a great tragedy indeed—you're headed for your sweetheart's room, not for the grave.

FAUST. What is heaven, in her arms? Even while I burn with her kisses, don't I always feel her need too? Am I not the fugitive, wandering without home or rest, the monster who, like a waterfall roaring down through rocks and gorges, hurls himself madly into the abyss? And there she is, off to the side, still innocent, still unawakened, living her simple, humble life in her little mountain cabin, her whole small world contained within it. And I, hated by God, wasn't satisfied until I'd dragged the stubborn rocks down and smashed them to dust! I have to undermine her and her peace too—Hell demanded this sacrifice, and now it has it! Help me, devil, get through what's coming; let whatever must happen, happen quickly! Let her fate fall on me, let it crush me too—let one single ruin bury both of us!

MEPHISTOPHELES. There it boils up again, there it burns again! You fool, go in and comfort her! When a head like yours can't see a way out, it always assumes the end must be near. Long live the man who keeps his nerve! Otherwise you wear the devil's own nature well enough—there's nothing in this world more pathetic than a devil in despair.

chapters.title: Margaret's Room
paragraphs: [At the spinning wheel, alone.]

MARGARET. My peace is gone, my heart is sore; I'll never find it again, never again, unless he's near me. Without him, it's like the grave—the whole world turns to bitterness and gall. My poor, weak mind is racked and crazed; my thoughts scatter, my senses reel. My peace is gone, my heart is sore; I'll never find it again, never again. Just to see him—only him—I sit at the window; just to meet him—only him—I leave the house. His proud walk, his noble build, the smile on his lips, the power in his eyes, the spell of his voice when he talks, the joy of his hand around mine, and oh—his kiss! My peace is gone, my heart is sore; I'll never find it again, never again. My whole heart aches for him alone. If only I dared hold him, and keep him, and never let go—kiss his mouth exactly as I please, and die, at last, in his kisses!

chapters.title: Martha's Garden
paragraphs: [Margaret. Faust.]
MARGARET. Promise me, Henry—
FAUST. Whatever I can!
MARGARET. Tell me—how do you feel about religion? You're a good, warm-hearted man, but I don't think it means much to you.
FAUST. Leave that be, my child! You know how much I love you; I'd give my blood, my life, for love. And as for church and faith, I won't take that away from anyone.
MARGARET. That's not enough—we have to actually believe in it.
FAUST. Do we?
MARGARET. If only I had some influence over you! And you don't even honor the holy sacraments.
FAUST. I do honor them.
MARGARET. But not because you want to. It's been ages since you've been to Mass or confession. Do you believe in God?
FAUST. My darling, who can dare say, 'I believe in God'? Ask any priest or any wise man, and their answer will sound like mockery of the person who asked.
MARGARET. So you don't believe, then!

FAUST. Don't misunderstand me, my sweet face! Who can truly name Him? Who can claim to believe in Him and say it plainly? And who, feeling and seeing Him everywhere, can deny Him and say, I don't believe? He who holds everything, upholds everything—doesn't he hold and uphold you, and me, and himself? Doesn't the sky arch above us? Doesn't the earth lie firm beneath our feet? Don't the eternal stars rise, gently shining down on us? Am I not looking into your eyes right now, and don't you feel it crowding into your head and heart, that force, forever weaving its eternal mystery, invisible and visible, all around you? Fill your heart with all of that, as vast as it is, and when you're utterly happy in the feeling of it, call it whatever you like—call it joy, call it heart, call it love, call it God! I have no name for it. Feeling is everything; a name is just noise and smoke, clouding over heaven's clear light.
MARGARET. That all sounds fine and good—the preacher says something quite similar, just with slightly different words.
FAUST. Everyone under the sun says the same thing, each in their own language—so why shouldn't I say it in mine?
MARGARET. Put that way, it seems reasonable enough. And yet something's still wrong, because you have no real Christianity.
FAUST. Dearest love!
MARGARET. It's troubled me for a long time, seeing you keep the company you keep.
FAUST. How do you mean?
MARGARET. That man who's always with you—I hate him, down in the depths of my soul. Nothing in my whole life has ever hit me with such a sharp stab of disgust as his repulsive face.
FAUST. Don't be afraid of him, sweetheart!

MARGARET. Just having him near feels like something bad to me. I'm kindly disposed to nearly everyone, but as much as my heart longs to see you, that man fills me with a secret horror. I really think he's a scoundrel—God forgive me if I'm wrong about him!
FAUST. Well, there have to be strange birds like that in the world.

MARGARET. I could never live with someone like him! The moment he steps through the door, he looks around with that sneer, half angry at everything—you can tell nothing in the world interests him. It's written right on his forehead that he can't stand the idea of love. I'm so happy on your arm, so free, so at ease, so warm—but when he's around, my heart feels choked.
FAUST. You angel, always sensing things before they happen!

MARGARET. It overwhelms me so much that wherever he comes across us, I feel as if I've stopped loving you. And when he's nearby, I can't even pray. It burns inside me like a flame—and I'm sure, Henry, you feel the same about him.
FAUST. Well, there's your prejudice against him!
MARGARET. But I have to go.
FAUST. Will there never be one quiet hour where we can be truly close, heart against heart, soul joined to soul?
MARGARET. If only I slept alone! I'd leave the bolt undone tonight for you. But my mother sleeps so lightly now, and if she ever caught us, it would be the death of me on the spot!
FAUST. Don't be afraid of that, angel! Here—a little vial. Just three drops of this in her drink, and she'll sink into the deepest sleep.
MARGARET. What wouldn't I do for you? It won't hurt her, will it, if I use it?
FAUST. Would I suggest it if it would, my love?
