MARGARET. Dearest, whenever I look at your face, I don't know what it is that makes me do whatever you ask. I've already done so much for you that there's hardly anything left to give. (Enter Mephistopheles.) [She exits.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. The little minx! Has she gone?
FAUST. Been spying again, have you?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I heard the whole thing—how thoroughly she's got you sized up. Seems the Doctor's been catechized. I hope it does you a world of good. Girls always want to check whether a man's as pious and proper as the old rules demand—if he'll follow along there, they think, he'll follow along everywhere else too.

FAUST. You monster—you'll never see or admit how this pure soul, so full of simple faith, so loving, so beyond words, torments herself with pious scruples over the one belief that means her salvation—terrified she might lose the man she loves so completely!
MEPHISTOPHELES. And you—full of sensual and supersensual longing—are being led around by the nose by a girl.
FAUST. You monstrosity, born of filth and fire!

MEPHISTOPHELES. And how expertly she reads faces, too! Around me she feels something, though she doesn't know what—she senses there's some hidden meaning behind this mask of mine. She feels I must be some kind of genius—maybe even the Devil himself! Well, well—tonight, then—?
FAUST. What business is that of yours?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, but it'll be quite a pleasure for me too!

chapters.title: At the Well
paragraphs: [Margaret and Lisbeth, carrying pitchers.]
LISBETH. Haven't you heard anything about Barbara?
MARGARET. No, not a word. I hardly go out at all.
LISBETH. It's true—Sibylla told me today. She's finally made a fool of herself, no doubt about it. And after putting on such airs!
MARGARET. What do you mean?
LISBETH. It's obvious! Whenever she eats or drinks, she's feeding two.
MARGARET. Oh!

LISBETH. So it serves her right, in the end. She clung to that fellow so long, so tightly! Such promenading they did! Parading around at village fairs and dances! They always had to be the center of attention, and he always treated her to pies and wine, and she made such a fuss with her pretty face. She behaved so shamelessly, so cheaply—taking every gift that fellow gave her. It was kissing and coddling, on and on and on! And now, in the end, she's lost her flower.
MARGARET. Poor, poor girl!

LISBETH. You pity her, after all that? While the rest of us sat spinning at home, and our mothers never let us out the door at night, she was off enjoying herself with her lover. Sitting on the doorstep, in the dark passageway, never once noticing how the hours passed. Well, now she won't be holding her head up—she'll be doing penance in church, in her sinner's smock!
MARGARET. Surely he'll marry her.
LISBETH. He'd be a fool to! A lively young man has plenty of other places to ply his trade. Besides, he's already left town.
MARGARET. That isn't right!
LISBETH. If she does manage to get him, she'd better watch out! The boys will tear her bridal wreath to pieces on the floor, and we'll scatter chaff in front of her door! [Exit.

MARGARET (walking home). How scornfully I used to condemn other girls, whenever some poor maiden was led astray! I could never find enough words to heap blame on other people's failings. However dark it seemed, I made it darker still, and in my heart I judged even more harshly than I spoke; and I congratulated myself and boasted of my own virtue—and now, I myself am a living sin! And yet—everything that led my heart to this, God! was so good, so dear, so true!

chapters.title: Zwinger
paragraphs: [In a niche in the wall stands a shrine holding an image of the Mater Dolorosa. Pots of flowers stand before it.]
[putting fresh flowers into the pots.]

MARGARET. Bend down to me, O Maiden, weighed down with sorrow, and turn your merciful face toward my pain! With the sword piercing your heart, aching with anguish, you look up to where your Son hangs slain! You see the Father; your grieving sighs rise up, carrying your sorrow and his pain aloft with them! Ah, the pain that wrings my flesh and bone is beyond guessing, beyond words! Why this heart of mine burns with such dread, why it trembles, why it aches with longing—only you know, you alone! Wherever I go, what grief, what misery and sorrow ache inside my breast! Alone, and oh, unable to sleep, I weep and weep and weep, and my heart is breaking. The flowerpots outside my window—alas, my tears wet them, as I set these flowers out for you in the early morning. Sitting in my lonely room, the morning sun shone red, and I sat there already in utter sorrow, still on my bed. Help me! Save me from death and disgrace! O Maiden, weighed down with sorrow, turn your face toward my pain!

chapters.title: Night. Street before Margaret's Door
paragraphs: VALENTINE (a soldier, Margaret's brother). Whenever I sat at some drinking party, where everyone got to boast to everyone else, and plenty of comrades praised their own pretty girls to me with real relish, glasses brimming over as they raised their toasts, elbows planted on the table as if daring anyone to argue—I would sit there, perfectly at ease, and listen to the bragging pile up. Then, stroking my beard, I'd say, smiling, the full glass in my hand: 'Each is well enough, in her own way. But is there anyone in the whole country like my sister Margaret, good as gold—one who could even hold a candle to her?' Clink, clank! 'Here's to her!' went round the table. 'He's telling the truth!' some cried. 'She's the flower of womanhood!' And all the braggarts fell silent. And now!—I could tear my hair out in fury, and dash my own brains out in despair! Now any low scamp can turn up his nose at me, can disgrace me with sneers and cutting taunts, and I sit there like a bankrupt debtor, sweating at any careless word dropped in passing! And yet, however much I'd like to thrash the lot of them, I can't even call them liars. But what's this sneaking into view over there? If I'm not mistaken, there are two of them. If one of them is him, let me at him! He won't leave this spot alive.
[Faust. Mephistopheles.]

FAUST. Look how, from the sacristy window, the eternal lamp sends its glow upward, fading sideways into ever fainter dimness, until the darkness closes in from the sky above! Just so do the shadows gather within my own heart.

MEPHISTOPHELES. I feel more like a sentimental tomcat, prowling around the tall fire-ladders and creeping stealthily along the rooftop coping: perfectly virtuous, all told, just a little thieving and a little playful. I can feel it in every limb—the anticipation building toward the great Walpurgis Night. The day after tomorrow brings its message, and then one stays up gladly, keeping watch.
FAUST. Meanwhile, might that treasure have risen to the surface yet—the one I see glimmering back there?
MEPHISTOPHELES. You'll soon have the pleasure of lifting the kettle out with its treasure inside. I took a peek in there recently—saw magnificent lion-dollars in it.
FAUST. Not even a single jewel, not one ring, to adorn my darling girl with?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Among the rest I saw something that looked like it might be a pearl necklace.
FAUST. That's good news indeed! It pains me to visit her without bringing any gift.

MEPHISTOPHELES. You shouldn't find it so annoying to enjoy something without giving anything back in return. Now, while the sky leads out its throng of stars, you'll hear a masterpiece—nothing could be more complete: I'll sing her a moral little song first, all the better to deceive her afterward. What are you doing here, in the clear light of dawn, dear Kathrina, standing before your lover's door? Beware! A young man lets a girl in as a maiden, but she who goes out again a maiden—never happens! Steer clear of his coaxing! Once it's done, good night to you, poor thing! Love's season is brief: don't be warm and willing to any thief, unless it comes with a wedding ring!
[He sings, accompanying himself on the cittern.]
VALENTINE (stepping forward). Who do you think you're luring? By God! You rat-catching piper—damn you! To the devil with the instrument first! And to the devil with the cursed musician next!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The cittern's smashed! It's fit for nothing else now.
VALENTINE. There's still a skull left for me to split!
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). Doctor, don't back away, I beg you! Stand your ground: I'll lead if you just stay close. Draw your sword, no delay! All you need to do is lunge—I'll parry.
VALENTINE. Then parry this!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Why not? It's easy. VALENTINE. And that one too!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Of course.
VALENTINE. I could swear the Devil himself is fighting! How can this be? My hand's already going numb—
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). Strike home!
VALENTINE (falling). Oh, God!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now the brute's been tamed! But come, let's go! It's time for us to flee—there's a cry of murder going up now. We could easily settle things with the police, but the criminal court will dig into this one and sift it through.
[He exits with Faust.]
MARTHA (at the window). Come out! Come out!
MARGARET (at the window). Quick, bring a light!
MARTHA (still at the window). They're cursing and raging, shouting and fighting!
PEOPLE. Look—here lies one already dead!
MARTHA (coming out of the house). Which way did the murderers run?
MARGARET (coming outside). Who's lying here?
PEOPLE. It's your own mother's son!
MARGARET. Almighty God! What misery!

VALENTINE. I'm dying! It's quickly said, and it'll be done even quicker. Why are you women wailing there? Instead, come here and listen, all of you! Margaret, look at you—still young, but not the least bit wise or sensible, to have handled your affairs so carelessly. So here's my advice, take it to heart: now that you're truly a whore, well then, be one outright!
[Everyone gathers around him.]
MARGARET. My brother! God—such words, to me?

VALENTINE. Leave our Lord God out of this business! What's done is done, alas—what follows from it has to happen too. You start secretly with one man, and soon others will come to you, and once a dozen have known you, you'll be free to the whole town besides. When Shame is first born, she comes into the world in secret, and they draw the veil of night over her head and ears; they're loath, in truth, to let her live at all. But let her grow up and gain her strength, and she'll walk abroad unveiled in broad daylight, without having grown one bit prettier for it. The uglier she looks, the more she seeks out the open light of day. I can already foresee the time when every honest person will turn away from you, you slut, and shrink from you as from a corpse that spreads infection. Your guilty heart will fail you then, the moment they look you in the face—you won't be decked out in a golden chain, you won't take your place at the altar! You won't dance and make merry dressed in lace and flowing ribbons! No, you'll hide in some corner, poor wretch, among the beggars and the cripples; and so, even if God forgives you, you'll live out a damned existence here on earth!
MARTHA. Commend your soul to God for pardon, for hardening your heart with such slander!
VALENTINE. You infamous pimp, be quiet! If I could kill that withered body of yours, it would earn me, for all my sinful pleasures, forgiveness in the richest measure.
MARGARET. My brother! This is torment straight out of Hell!
VALENTINE. I tell you, hold back your tears! When you turned away from honor, it stabbed me straight to the heart. Now, through the sleep of the grave, I go to God as a brave soldier goes.
[He dies.]

chapters.title: Cathedral
paragraphs: [A church service is underway: organ music and a choral anthem.]
[Margaret sits among a large congregation; the Evil Spirit stands behind her.]

EVIL SPIRIT. How different it was, Margaret, when you came to this altar still innocent, and babbled your prayers from that worn, well-thumbed prayer book—half childish play, half God alive within you! Margaret! Where do your thoughts wander now? What hidden crime lies in your heart? Are you praying for mercy on your mother's soul, who fell into her long, long torment—and through you? Whose blood is that on your doorstep? And isn't something stirring, quickening, beneath your own heart, unsettling your life with its ominous presence?
MARGARET. Oh, misery! If only I were free of these thoughts that cross my mind, pulling me this way and that, no matter how I resist!
CHORUS. Dies irae, dies illa, solvet saeclum in favilla! (The organ sounds.)
EVIL SPIRIT. Wrath seizes you! The trumpet sounds! The graves tremble! And your heart, roused up again out of its ashen rest into fiery torment, throbs back to life!
MARGARET. If only I were out of here! I feel as though this organ is taking the very breath from my body, as if the anthem is dissolving my heart within me!

CHORUS. Judex ergo cum sedebit, quidquid latet apparebit, nil inultum remanebit. MARGARET. I cannot breathe! These massive pillars are imprisoning me! These vaulted arches are crushing me down!—Air, give me air!
EVIL SPIRIT. Hide yourself away! Sin and shame never stay hidden. Air? Light? Woe to you!
CHORUS. Quid sum miser tunc dicturus, quem patronem rogaturus, cum vix justus sit securus?
EVIL SPIRIT. They turn their faces from you—the glorified ones. The pure shudder and refuse to hold out their hands to you! Woe to you!
CHORUS. Quid sum miser tunc dicturus?
MARGARET. Neighbor—your smelling salts! (She faints.)

chapters.title: Walpurgis-Night
paragraphs: [The Harz Mountains. The district around Schierke and Elend.]
[Faust. Mephistopheles.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Wouldn't you like the help of a broomstick to ride? I'd gladly find you the sturdiest billy-goat around—the way ahead of us still has some distance to go.

FAUST. As long as I still feel fresh life in my legs, this knotted walking stick is all I need. Why shorten the way at all? Wandering through this labyrinth of valleys, then climbing those rocky ramparts up ahead, where the fountain flings its endless spray—it's such a delight that I'd rather my steps lingered. Spring is stirring in the fragrant birches, and even the fir tree feels it now: should our own limbs escape its gentle touch?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I feel nothing of the kind, I swear! Winter still rules my body—I'd rather have frost and snow along my path. How mournfully the moon's disk rises, incomplete and reddish, its glow arriving late, lighting things so dimly that at every step one bangs into a rock or a tree! Let's make use of a will-o'-the-wisp's glow instead: I see one over there, burning merrily. Hey there, my friend! I'll press you into service: why waste your brightness so pointlessly? Be good enough to light our way up this slope!
WILL-O'-THE-WISP. Out of respect for you, I hope, I'll manage to curb my unsteady temperament—though zigzag paths are what we're used to keeping.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Is that so? He wants to imitate mankind, does he! Now, in the Devil's name, go straight, or I'll snuff out that flickering little spark of your existence!

WILL-O'-THE-WISP. You're clearly the master of this house, I can tell, and I'll do my best to serve you properly. But do bear in mind: the mountain is mad with magic tonight, and if a will-o'-the-wisp is going to guide you along the way, you mustn't expect too much precision. It seems we've just crossed newly into the realm of enchanted dreams. Do as you like, then, and guide us truly, so our feet keep moving forward through these vast, empty spaces! Look how swiftly everything changes places—tree after tree comes trooping past us, and crags stoop down over us, and rocky snouts jut out overhead—listen to them snoring, listen to them blowing! Over the stones, over the grasses, streams and rivulets flow down toward the hollow. Do I hear noises? Songs following after? Do I hear tender pleas of love? Voices out of some heavenly vision? Sounds of hope, of undying love! And the echoes come back faint and hollow, like old tales from days gone by. Hoo-hoo! Shoo-hoo! Nearer now hover the jay and the screech-owl, and the plover—are they all awake and crying out? Is that the salamander pushing its bloated belly through the bushes? And the roots, twisted like serpents, toiling through the sand and boulders, frighten us as they uncoil their strangest tangles to snare us, helpless: living knots and uncanny gnarls feel about with polyp-like tentacles for the wanderer. Mice go flying past, a thousand colors, streaming in herds through the moss and through the heather! And fireflies flicker and darken, crowding swarms that soar and sparkle, gathering around us in bewildering escort! Tell me, are we still standing still, or are we climbing further? Everything is turning, whirling, blending together—trees and rocks with grinning faces, wandering lights spinning in mazes, forever growing, forever spreading!
[Faust, Mephistopheles, Will-o'-the-Wisp.]
[singing in alternation.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Take hold of my coattail, and take heart! Here stands a middle peak, from which one can see, with astonishment, Mammon himself lighting up the mountainside.

FAUST. How strangely a dreary light glimmers through the hollows down there, like the light of dawn! Its haze follows and traces the deepest gorges, faint and pale. Here steam rises, there rolling vapor sweeps by; here the glow burns through mist and haze—now it creeps along like a delicate thread, now it leaps and plays like a fountain. Here it winds away and braids the valley into a hundred separate veins; there, squeezed into a corner and split apart, it detaches itself, spreads out, and fades. Here sparks gush out, glowing red-hot, like scattered showers of golden sand—but look! Up at their full height, right now, the rocky ramparts stand ablaze.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Hasn't Lord Mammon lit up his palace grandly for this festive night? You're lucky to have seen the sight—the boisterous guests who were invited are already on their way.
FAUST. How the storm rages through the air! With what fierce blows it's beating on my neck!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Take shelter under these old ribs of rock—hold on tight, or you'll be flung down into the chasms there! The night is black with mist; listen how the forests grind and crack! The frightened owls scatter; listen, the pillars are shattering! The evergreen palaces are shaking! Branches groan and break, the tree trunks thunder terribly, the roots are twisting apart! In a horrible, tangled crash, one tree after another comes down on top of the last, and over the wreckage-strewn gorges the storm whistles and surges! Do you hear voices ringing higher up? Far away, or singing nearer? Yes—all along the mountainside sweeps a furious, bewitching song!

WITCHES (in chorus). The witches ride up to the Brocken's summit; the stubble is yellow, and the crop is green. There the crowd gathers for its carnival: Lord Urian sits over them all. And so they go, over stone and stump; the witch she——s, and——s the goat.
A VOICE. Old Baubo comes now, all alone; she's riding on a farrow sow.
CHORUS. Honor, then, to whom honor is due! Let Dame Baubo lead the crew! A tough old sow, with the mother astride her, and then follow the witches, every one.
A VOICE. Which way did you come here?
VOICE. Over the Ilsenstein. I peeked in at the owl alone in her nest—how she stared and glared!
VOICE. Go to Hell! Why in such a fierce hurry?
VOICE. She's scratched me and flayed me—look at the wounds she's given me!

WITCHES (chorus). The way is wide, the way is long: look what a wild and crazy mob! The broom scratches, the pitchfork jabs, the child is smothered, the mother bursts open. WIZARDS (semi-chorus). We crawl along like snails in their shells: the women are always ahead of us. When we head toward the Devil's house, a woman's a thousand steps in front.
OTHER SEMI-CHORUS. We don't measure things so carefully: a woman's thousand steps amount to cheating. However fast she hurries, a man clears the whole distance in a single leap.
VOICE (from above). Come on, come on, up from Rocky Lake!
VOICE (from below). We'd love to make our way up there. We've washed ourselves and are as bright as you could wish, and yet we're still eternally barren.
BOTH CHORUSES. The wind falls silent, a star shoots past. The dreary moon deserts the sky; the magic notes, spark after spark, drizzle down, whistling through the dark.
VOICE (from below). Halt there! Hey there!
VOICE (from above). Who's calling from that rocky cleft down there?
VOICE (from below). Take me too! Take me too! I've been climbing for three hundred years now, and still I can't see the summit: I want to be among my own kind.
BOTH CHORUSES. The broom carries, the staff carries, the pitchfork carries, the goat carries: whoever can't lift himself up tonight is a ruined creature forever.

HALF-WITCH (from below). I've been stumbling along so long, in such a sorry state, and the others are already so far ahead! At home I have neither rest nor cheer, and yet I still can't catch up with them here.
CHORUS OF WITCHES. A salve will cheer the witch up well; a rag will serve just fine as a sail; any old trough makes a decent ship; whoever doesn't fly tonight will never fly at all.
BOTH CHORUSES. When our flight has whirled around the summit, we'll sink lower and land on the ground; and far and wide we'll press down on the heather with swarms of wanton witchery!
[They settle to the ground.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. They crowd and shove, they roar and clatter! They whirl and whistle, tug and chatter! They glow, they spurt sparks, they stink, they burn! Now we're really getting a taste of true witch-nature. Stay close! Or we'll be separated in our turn—where are you?
FAUST (from a distance). Here!

MEPHISTOPHELES. What! Whirled so far off already? Then I'll have to use my authority as master of this house and clear the way. Make room! Squire Voland is coming through! Room, my gentle rabble, room! Here, Doctor, hold on to me: in one jump we'll get to a clearer space and free ourselves from the crowd—even for someone like me, this is too much. Over there, something is shining more brightly, with a special light, inside those bushes; I've a mind to go see. Come on, let's slip a little closer.

FAUST. Spirit of Contradiction! Lead on, I'll follow right behind. It strikes me as a very wise plan, if I judge rightly: we climb all the way to the top of the Brocken on Walpurgis Night, just so that we can isolate ourselves here, of all places.
MEPHISTOPHELES. But look, what a motley scattering of flames among the heather! There's a lively little club gathered together—in smaller circles, at least, one isn't alone.
FAUST. I must admit, the summit is better: up there I see fire and whirling smoke. They're seeking out the Evil One in wild confusion; many riddles might find their solution there.

MEPHISTOPHELES. But riddles get tangled up over there too. Leave the crowd to their own riot! Here we'll settle ourselves quietly. It's an old, well-established trade, this business of building little worlds within the bigger one. I see stark-naked young witches gathering, and old ones cunningly veiled and hidden: for my sake, be kind, and don't treat them rudely! The trouble is small, and the fun is great. I can hear instruments being tuned up—a vile racket, but one has to learn to put up with the crooning. Come, come along! It has to be done, I insist! I'll go ahead and introduce you there, and you'll owe me a new favor for it. That's no small space over there, what do you say, my friend? Look over there—you can barely make out where it ends: a hundred fires are burning along the ranks. They dance, they chat, they cook, they drink, they court: now tell me, where could you find better sport than that?
FAUST. To get us into the revelry, will you play the part of a wizard, or of a devil?

MEPHISTOPHELES. It's true, I'm mostly used to going incognito—but on a gala day, a man may show off his decorations. The Order of the Garter doesn't adorn my suit, but here the cloven hoof is honored and right at home. Do you see that snail over there? It comes on, slow and steady; its feelers probe so delicately that it's already caught my scent: there's no disguising myself here, however I try. But come! We'll move from this fire to a newer one: I'll be the go-between, and you the suitor. Old gentlemen, why linger at the edges? Come in! I'd praise you more if I found you tucked snugly into the center, with youth and revelry wrapped all around you like a belt: each of you gets plenty of being alone at home already.
[To some men sitting around dying embers.]
GENERAL. Tell me, who would put any trust in nations, however much one has worked and planned on their behalf? For with the common people, just as with women, youth always has the upper hand.
MINISTER. They've strayed too far now from what's just and wise. I praise the old days, and not without reason: back when we were the ones running everything, that was truly the golden age.
PARVENU. We weren't stupid either, back in our day, and we often did what we shouldn't have. But now everything has slid off its foundations, right when we meant to hold it all firmly together.

AUTHOR. Who, nowadays, will read a work of moderate good sense? Such books are considered old-fashioned and mossy; and as for the younger generation, they've truly never been so cheeky and impertinent before.
[Mephistopheles, who suddenly appears very old.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. I can feel that mankind is ripe for Judgment Day. This is the last time I've climbed the witches' hill: since my own cask has been drained to the dregs, the world's must surely soon be finished too.

HUCKSTER-WITCH. Gentlemen, don't just walk past me like that! Don't miss your chance! Take a good look at my wares—my stock is rare and varied. And yet there's nothing I've collected here—you won't find a shop like this anywhere on earth!—that hasn't, at some point, inflicted grievous harm on the world and on mankind. There's no dagger here that hasn't set blood flowing; no cup that hasn't once poured swift death, glowing with poison, into some healthy body; no gem that hasn't brought some girl to shame; no sword that hasn't severed some unsuspecting bond, or struck an enemy down from behind.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Old gossip, you understand the times badly: what's done has already happened—what happens now is done as it comes! You'd do better to send us something new: only novelty can win us over now.
FAUST. Don't let me lose myself in all this commotion! This is a fair unlike any there's ever been!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The whirlpool swirls to rise to the top: you get shoved along yourself, all the while imagining that you're the one doing the shoving.
FAUST. But who's that?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Take special notice of her—that's Lilith.
FAUST. Who?

MEPHISTOPHELES. She's Adam's first wife. Beware the snare hidden in her lovely hair, her single, splendid ornament! Once she manages to trap a young man with it, she won't free him from her leash again anytime soon.
FAUST. Those two over there, the old one sitting with the young one—they've already danced longer than is fitting.
MEPHISTOPHELES. No rest tonight, for young or old! They're starting another dance: come now, let's join in!
FAUST (dancing with the young witch). A lovely dream once came to me; I saw an apple tree in it, and on it two of the fairest apples gleamed: they tempted me so much that I climbed up after them.
THE FAIR ONE. You men have desired apples ever since they first grew in Paradise; and it moves me with joy to know that such apples grow in my garden too.
MEPHISTOPHELES (dancing with the old one). A dissolute dream once came to me too: in it I saw a tree, split down the middle, which had a——; but crude as it was, I liked it well enough.
THE OLD ONE. Here I offer my warmest greeting to the knight with the cloven foot! Let him get a——ready, if a——doesn't frighten him off.

PROKTOPHANTASMIST. Accursed rabble! How dare you carry on like this? Haven't you had proof enough, long ago, that ghosts can't stand on ordinary ground? And now here you are, even dancing, as if you were one of us!
THE FAIR ONE (dancing). Then why does he even come to our ball?

FAUST (dancing). Oh, everyone comes down hard on him! Whenever others dance, he has to weigh in on it: if he can't chatter about every single step, then as far as he's concerned it's as if the step were never taken; but if you dance forward at all, his temper flares up worst of all. If you'd only whirl around in the same regular circles he grinds out in his dull old mill, he'd show some goodwill at least—especially if you listened and took his lecturing to heart.

PROKTOPHANTASMIST. You're still here? This is unheard of! Vanish at once! We've already spoken the enlightening word. This pack of devils won't be governed by any rules: we're so wise, and yet Tegel is still haunted. How I have swept and stirred, trying to clear out this folly! It will never be clean—why, it's simply unheard of!
THE FAIR ONE. Then stop boring us at our ball!

PROKTOPHANTASMIST. I tell you, spirits, right to your faces—I allow no room for the despotism of spirits; my own spirit simply can't stand for it. I see that nothing's going to succeed amid such revelry; but I always salvage something from my travels, and I hope, before my final step into the grave, to get the better of the poets and the devils both.
[The dance continues.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. He'll go sit himself down in the nearest puddle now; that's the one comfort he can always rely on: and once the leeches are hanging off his backside, gorging themselves silly, he'll be cured of spirits, and of Spirit both. But why have you abandoned the lovely maiden who was singing so sweetly in the dance?
[To Faust, who has stepped away from the dance.]
FAUST. Ah—right in the middle of it, a red mouse leapt out of her mouth. Reason enough.
MEPHISTOPHELES. That's nothing! One shouldn't be so squeamish—so the mouse wasn't gray, and that's enough to put you off? Who thinks about that sort of thing, in love's chosen season?
FAUST. Then I saw—
MEPHISTOPHELES. What?

FAUST. Mephisto, do you see, over there, alone and far off, a girl most pale and fair? She stumbles forward, hardly seeming to know her way, as if her feet were fettered and held her back. I must confess, it seems to me as though it were my own dear Margaret.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Leave that alone! Everyone who's gone near it has come away worse for it: it's a magic phantom, a lifeless image with no soul in it. It's no good encountering such a thing: its blank, fixed stare numbs human blood, and turns a person almost to stone. You know the story of Medusa.
FAUST. Truly, those are the eyes of someone who died with no loving hand to close them; that is the breast I once lay against—the sweet body beside which I used to rest!
MEPHISTOPHELES. It's all magic, you fool, so easily seduced! To every man she appears to be his own beloved.
FAUST. The anguish, the rapture, ensnare me so that I cannot tear myself away from her gaze! And, strangely, around her lovely throat a single scarlet band gleams, no wider than the blade of a knife!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Quite right! I notice the mark too. She sometimes carries her own head under her arm—Perseus lopped it off, her old adversary. And still you crave the same illusion! Come, let's climb up this little hill; even the Prater shows no livelier bustle than this, and unless my senses have been bewitched, I do believe I see a theater. What's going on there? SERVIBILIS. It's about to start up again—a new performance, the last of seven. It's the custom here to put on that number. It was written by an amateur, and amateurs play all the parts. Now, if you'll forgive me, I must vanish: as the amateur, it's my job to raise the curtain. MEPHISTOPHELES. Whenever I meet you up on the Blocksberg, I find that fitting—since that's exactly where you belong.

chapters.title: Walpurgis-Night's Dream
paragraphs: [Oberon and Titania's Golden Wedding Anniversary. An Intermezzo.]
MANAGER. Sons of Mieding, rest today! There's no need for your stage machinery: a misty valley and a gray mountain—that's all the scenery we need.
HERALD. For a wedding to be golden, fifty years must have passed. But give me the gold once the quarreling's settled.
OBERON. Spirits, if you're here, let yourselves be seen—show yourselves, and be glad! The fairy king and fairy queen have just renewed their vows.
PUCK. Here comes Puck, light on his feet, whisking and whirling in time: a hundred more come after him, to share in his pleasure.
ARIEL. Ariel's song is pure as heaven, his notes are sweet and rare: he may draw in ugly faces too, but it's the beautiful ones he truly charms.
OBERON. Married couples who wish to get along—learn from how we ourselves were matched! If your pairs want to be loving, first you must be separated!
TITANIA. If a wife is ruled by her whims, and nags at her husband, take him off to the North Pole, and her to the Equator!
ORCHESTRA (all together, fortissimo). Flies' snouts, mosquito bills, and every kind of kin, frogs in the grass, crickets chirping—these are our musicians!
SOLO. Look, there's the bagpipe following along—it's a soap bubble blown up big: hear the snickety-snackety sound coming through his double nostrils!
SPIRIT, JUST TAKING SHAPE. A spider's foot, a toad's fat belly, and little wings—we know them well! It won't turn out to be much of a creature, but it will make a nice little poem.
A LITTLE COUPLE. Little steps and lofty leaps through honeydew and fragrance: with all your tripping and wandering, you'll never climb the airy heights.
INQUISITIVE TRAVELER. Is this only a masquerade? Am I seeing this clearly? Oberon, that beautiful spirit, appears before my very eyes tonight!
ORTHODOX. I see no claw, no tail on him! And yet, beyond any argument, like 'the Gods of Greece,' he too must be some kind of devil.
NORTHERN ARTIST. I'm only catching a few sketchy outlines of this whole tournament; but I'm already preparing myself in good time for my journey to Italy.
PURIST. My bad luck has brought me here, alas! How the orgy roars on, louder and louder! And out of the whole mass of witches, only two of them are wearing powder.
YOUNG WITCH. Powder suits a gray, wrinkled old fool, same as a petticoat does; so I sit naked on my goat instead, and show off a strapping young body.
MATRON. We have far too much tact and good sense to trade insults with a scold; but tender and young as you are, I hope to see you rot away yet.
LEADER OF THE BAND. Flies' snouts and mosquito bills, don't swarm so thick around the naked ones! Frogs in the grass, crickets chirping—keep the time, and keep it well!
WEATHERCOCK (turning to one side). Company exactly to one's taste! Brides only, and the sweetest ones! And bachelors full of youth and fire, and the most complete prospects imaginable!
WEATHERCOCK (turning to the other side). And if the earth doesn't open up right now to swallow every one of these ranters, then I swear I'll jump straight into hell myself, this instant!
XENIES. See us here as little insects, flitting about with our sharpest little pincers, so that we may honor our Papa Satan as is only fitting.
HENNINGS. Look how, massed together in crowds, they carry on joking so shamelessly! They'll even claim, in the end, that their hearts are perfectly innocent.
MUSAGETES. Amid this witches' revelry, one loses one's way quite gladly; and truly, it would be easier to do that than to command the Muses.
FORMER GENIUS OF THE AGE. The right sort of people always praise one's talents: come on, then, and none shall get past us! The Blocksberg has a broad summit, just like Germany's own Parnassus.
INQUISITIVE TRAVELER. Tell me, who's that stiff, pompous man? He walks with such haughty steps: he sniffs at everything he possibly can—'he's on the scent of the Jesuits' trail.'
CRANE. Clear streams and muddy ones alike suit me fine for fishing and sport: and that's why you see even a pious man here, keeping company with devils.
WORLDLING. Yes, I suspect that for the pious, any instrument at all will serve their purpose; and up on the Blocksberg they've set up plenty of meeting places of their own.
DANCER. A newer chorus takes over now! I hear drumming in the distance. 'Don't be alarmed—it's only the bittern, booming away as always, down in the reeds.'
DANCING-MASTER. Look how each one lifts his legs in a nimble little trip, clearing space for himself! Crooked jumps, heavy hops—and not one of them cares how it looks.
GOOD FELLOW. This rabble is held together by such hatred, that maiming and killing delight them: just as Orpheus's lyre once compelled the beasts, here it's the bagpipe that unites them.
DOGMATIST. I won't be led astray by any lure of doubts or critical quibbles: the Devil must surely be something real—otherwise how could there be devils at all?
IDEALIST. Just this once, the fantasy working in me is really too tyrannical: truly, if I am all that I see, then I must be an idiot!
REALIST. This racket and fuss on every side gives me great vexation; and for the first time, here I stand on ground that isn't secure at all.
SUPERNATURALIST. I watch this whole show with great delight, and grant these creatures their due merits, since from the devils here I can also infer the existence of better spirits.
SKEPTIC. They chase after that flame, on and on, thinking they're close to the treasure: but Devil rhymes only with Doubt, so I'm quite content to be here.
LEADER OF THE BAND. Frogs in the green, crickets chirping—such amateurs, damn it all! Flies' snouts and mosquito bills—every one of them a fine musician!
THE ADROIT ONES. We call our clan of merry creatures 'without a care,' then; we can't walk on our feet anymore, so we go along on our heads instead.
THE AWKWARD ONES. Once we sponged off plenty of good bits, but now, God help us, that's all over: our shoes are danced clean through, we suppose, and we've nothing left but bare soles to run on.
WILL-O'-THE-WISPS. We come up out of the marshes, where we first originated; and yet here in these ranks, all at once, we're rated as glittering gallants.
SHOOTING STAR. I came darting down here from the sky, shooting along in starlight and fire; now I lie crosswise in the grass—who'll help me back onto my feet?
THE HEAVY FELLOWS. Room! Make room all around us! The grass is getting trampled: spirits are coming too, and they're bulky masses of them.
PUCK. Don't come lumbering in so stall-fed, like elephant calves all around one! And let the heaviest weight tonight be Puck himself, the stout one!
ARIEL. If loving Nature, or the Mind, unfolds its wings behind you, then follow my airy path up to the mount of roses!
ORCHESTRA (pianissimo). The cloud and trailing mist overhead are lit up now: a breath stirs in the leaves, a wind stirs in the reeds, and everything dissolves away.

chapters.title: A Gloomy Day. Open Country
paragraphs: [Faust and Mephistopheles.]

FAUST. In misery! In despair! Wretchedly astray on the face of the earth for so long, and now imprisoned! That gracious, ill-fated creature, shut up in a dungeon like a criminal, handed over to horrible torments! It has come to this—to this!—You treacherous, contemptible spirit, and you hid it from me!—Stand there, then—stand! Roll your devilish eyes in fury all you like! Stand there and defy me with your unbearable presence! Imprisoned! In misery beyond any remedy! Handed over to evil spirits, and to a cold, condemning humanity! And all the while you lulled me with the most shallow amusements, hid her worsening wretchedness from me, and let her go helplessly to ruin!
MEPHISTOPHELES. She isn't the first.

FAUST. Dog! Abominable monster! Transform him back, Infinite Spirit—transform the reptile back into his dog's shape, the one he loved to wear at night, scampering along ahead of me, rolling himself at the feet of some unsuspecting wanderer, and hanging on his shoulders when he stumbled! Turn him back into that favorite shape of his, so he can crawl on his belly in the dust before me—so that I can trample him underfoot, the outlaw that he is! Not the first! Oh, the grief—grief no human soul can grasp—that more than one being should sink into the depths of this misery, that the first one's writhing death-agony, under the eyes of the Eternal Forgiver, did not atone for the guilt of all the rest! The misery of this one single girl cuts straight to the marrow of my life; and you sit there calmly grinning at the fate of thousands!

MEPHISTOPHELES. So here we are, already at the end of our wits again, where you men's understanding runs wild. Why did you enter into partnership with us, if you can't see it through? You want to fly, but you can't handle the dizziness? Did we force ourselves on you, or did you force yourself on us?

FAUST. Don't grind your ravenous teeth at me like that! It fills me with horrible disgust. Mighty, glorious Spirit, who granted me your presence, who knows my heart and my soul, why chain me to this criminal companion, who feeds on mischief and gorges himself on ruin?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Are you finished?
FAUST. Rescue her, or woe to you! Let the most terrible curse fall on you for thousands of ages!

MEPHISTOPHELES. I cannot loosen the Avenger's chains, or undo his bolts. Rescue her? Who was it that plunged her into ruin—I, or you? Do you want to seize hold of the thunder itself? It's a good thing that's not been given to you miserable mortals! Crushing the innocent bystander to pieces—that's the tyrant's way of getting himself out of an embarrassment.
[FAUST looks around wildly.]
FAUST. Take me there! She will be free!

MEPHISTOPHELES. And the danger you'll be exposing yourself to? Know that the guilt of blood from your own hand still lies over that town! Avenging spirits hover over the spot where the victim fell, and lie in wait for the murderer's return.
FAUST. That too, from you? May the murder and death of a whole world fall upon you, monster! Take me there, I tell you, and set her free!

MEPHISTOPHELES. I will carry you there; now listen to what I can do! Do I have all the power in Heaven and on Earth? I'll cloud the jailer's senses, get hold of the key, and lead her out with a human hand! I'll keep watch; the magic horses are ready, and I'll carry you both off. That much is within my power.
FAUST. Up, and away!

chapters.title: Night. Open Field
paragraphs: [Faust and Mephistopheles speeding onward on black horses.]
FAUST. What are they weaving there, around the raven-stone?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I don't know what they're brewing, or what they're up to.
FAUST. Soaring up, swooping down, bowing and bending!
MEPHISTOPHELES. A coven of witches.
FAUST. They're scattering something—consecrating, cursing!
MEPHISTOPHELES. On! On!

chapters.title: Dungeon
paragraphs: [Faust, carrying a bunch of keys and a lamp, stands before an iron door.]

FAUST. A shudder comes over me, one I haven't felt in a long time; all humanity's collected grief overwhelms me here. She lives within these dark, damp walls before me, and her whole crime was nothing but a dear delusion! What—am I hesitating to free her? Am I afraid to see her again? On, then! My shrinking back only brings death closer. 'My mother, the whore, who put me to death; my father, the scoundrel, who ate me up! My little sister, so good, laid my bones out in the wood, in the damp moss and clay: then I became a beautiful bird of the woods; fly away! Fly away!'
[He grasps the lock: the sound of singing is heard inside.]

FAUST (unlocking the door). She has no idea her lover is listening close by, that he can hear the rattling chain, the rustling straw. MARGARET (hiding herself on the pallet). Oh, misery! They're coming. O bitter death! FAUST (whispering). Hush, hush! The hour has come that will set you free. MARGARET (throwing herself before him). If you're a man, then have pity on my distress! FAUST. Your cries will wake the guards, and they'll seize you! (He takes hold of her fetters to unlock them.)
[He enters.]

MARGARET (on her knees). Who gave you such power over me, executioner? You've come for me at the midnight hour: have mercy on me, let me live! Won't it be soon enough once the morning bell has rung? And I'm still so young, so young! And now death is coming, and ruin! I too was pretty once, and that was my undoing. My love was close by, but now he's far away; my wreath lies torn, my blossoms are scattered. Don't seize me so violently! Spare me! What have I done to you? Don't let me beg you in vain! In all my life, I never once happened to meet you!
[She rises.]
FAUST. Can I possibly survive this misery?

MARGARET. I'm entirely in your power now. But let me nurse my baby first! I blessed it, all through this long night; they took it away from me, to torment me, maybe, and now they say I killed the child outright. And I'll never be happy again. They sing songs about me!—it's a wicked thing for people to do! There's an old story with the very same refrain; who told them to read it that way?
FAUST (falling to his knees). Here kneels one who loves you always, come to break the chains of your suffering.

MARGARET (throwing herself down beside him). Oh, let us kneel and call on the saints to hide us! Beneath the steps beside us, under the threshold, Hell is heaving with thunder! The Evil One, in terrible wrath, is searching for a way to find his prey!
FAUST (aloud). Margaret! Margaret!

MARGARET (listening intently). That was my lover's voice! Where is he? I heard him call my name. I'm free! No one shall enslave me now. I'll fly to throw my arms around his neck, I'll lie against his chest! He stood on the threshold, calling 'Margaret!'—amid Hell's howling and its appalling noise, amid the wrathful, infernal mockery, I knew the sweet sound of that beloved voice!
[She springs to her feet: the fetters fall off.]
FAUST. It's me!

MARGARET. It's you! Oh, say it again! It's him, it's him! Where has all my pain gone now—the anguish of this dungeon, and the chains? It's you! You've come to save me, and I am saved!—I see the street again, where I first laid eyes on you; and the garden, all in bloom, where Martha and I would wait for you to come.
[Clasping him.]
FAUST (trying to pull her along). Come! Come with me!
MARGARET. Wait, now! I'm so glad to stay, when you stay with me!
[Caressing him.]
FAUST. Away now! If you linger here any longer, we'll pay dearly for it.

MARGARET. Kiss me!—can't you do even that anymore? My friend, you've only been gone such a short time, and you've already forgotten how to kiss? Why does my heart feel so anxious, here against your chest? Once your glances made a heaven for me, once your loving words spoke a heaven to me, and you used to kiss me as if you meant to smother me with kisses—kiss me! Or I'll kiss you! Oh, misery—your lips are cold, and still. How changed your passion is now! Who has done this to me?
[She embraces him.]
[She turns away from him.]
FAUST. Come, follow me! My darling, have more courage: soon I'll hold you close with a thousandfold warmth; but follow me now! That's all I ask of you.
MARGARET (turning back to him). And is it really you? You, surely, truly?
FAUST. It's me! Come on!
MARGARET. You'll loosen my chains, and take me into your arms once more. How is it that you don't shrink away from me?—Tell me, my friend, do you even know who it is you're setting free?
FAUST. Come! Come! The night is already fading.

MARGARET. I've put my own mother to death; I've drowned the baby that was born to you and me. Wasn't it given to the two of us? You too!—It's you! It hardly seems real—give me your hand! This isn't a dream! Your dear, dear hand!—but, oh, it's wet! Wipe it off, then! I think there's still blood on it. Oh God, what have you done? No—put your sword away at last! Don't frighten me!
FAUST. Oh, let the past be past! Your words will be the death of me!

MARGARET. No, no! You must outlive us. Now let me tell you what graves to give us: tomorrow you must begin this work of sorrow! Give my mother the best place, then lay my brother close beside her, and put me a little way off—but not too far, I beg you! And here, at my right breast, lay my baby! No one else shall lie next to me!—Ah, hiding myself away in your arms, that was such a sweet and gracious bliss, but I can never have it again, never again! I want to force myself on you, to hold onto it, and yet you seem to push my kiss away: and still it's you, so good, so kind to look at!
FAUST. If you truly feel that it's me, then come with me!
MARGARET. Out there?
FAUST. To freedom.
MARGARET. If the grave is out there, if death is lying in wait, then come! From here to eternal rest—but not one step further, no, no! You're going away! Oh, Henry, if only I could go!
FAUST. You can! Just will it! The door stands open.

MARGARET. I don't dare go: there's no hope left for me anymore. Why should I flee? They'd only waylay me on my way! It's so wretched, to be forced to beg for a living, and a guilty conscience makes the misery even sharper! It's so wretched to be a stranger, forsaken, and still I'd be hunted down and caught!
FAUST. I'll stay with you, then.

MARGARET. Quick! Be quick! Save your dying child! Go! Follow the ridge, up along the brook, over the bridge, into the woods, to the left, where the plank lies across the pool! Seize it, quickly! It's trying to rise, it's still struggling! Save it! Save it!
FAUST. Gather your wandering wits! One step, and you're free at last!

MARGARET. If only we'd gotten past the mountain! There sits my mother, on a stone—an icy shiver runs through me! There sits my mother on a stone, and her head keeps wagging back and forth. She beckons—no, she isn't nodding, her heavy head just falls forward; she slept so long that she'll never wake again. She was sleeping, while we lay caressing each other: ah, those were the days of blessing!
FAUST. Words and prayers are worth nothing here; I'll venture, then, to carry you out myself.
MARGARET. No—let me go! I won't stand for force! Don't grip me so murderously! I've done everything else, for love of you.
FAUST. Day is dawning: dearest, dearest!

MARGARET. Day? Yes, the day is coming—the last day is breaking for me! It was supposed to be my wedding day! Tell no one that you've been with Margaret! Woe for my bridal garland! The chances are gone now—it's all in vain! We'll meet again once more, but not at any dance! The crowd is thronging, and not a word is spoken: the square below and the streets are overflowing: the death-bell tolls, the staff of office is broken. I am seized, and bound, and handed over—shoved to the block—they give the signal! The blade that now quivers over my neck has quivered over every neck before mine. The world lies silent, like the grave!
FAUST. Oh, if only I had never been born!
MEPHISTOPHELES (appearing outside). Away! Or you're lost before morning. It's useless, all this talking, delaying, and praying! My horses are neighing—morning twilight is near.
MARGARET. What's rising up out of the threshold there? Him! Him! Don't let him near! What does he want in this holy place? He's come for me!
FAUST. You shall live.
MARGARET. Judgment of God! I give myself over to you.
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). Come! Or I'll leave the two of you in the lurch!
MARGARET. I am yours, Father! Rescue me! You angels, you holy cohorts, guard me, camp around me, ward off all evil from me! Henry! I shudder to think of you.
MEPHISTOPHELES. She is judged!
VOICE (from above). She is saved!
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). Come here, to me!
[He vanishes, taking Faust with him.]
VOICE (from within, fading away). Henry! Henry!
